rationale: Adenosine-sensitive narrow-complex tachycardia that abruptly terminates is diagnostic of AVNRT or AVRT involving the AV node as part of the reentrant circuit. Clinical pearl: "Adenosine effect" — If tachycardia terminates, the AV node was part of the circuit (AVNRT/AVRT/WPW).

question: A 62-year-old with STEMI undergoes primary PCI to the LAD. Post-procedure day 62, develops sudden dyspnea and hypoxia. New pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla. CXR shows pulmonary edema. What is the most likely complication?

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2-7 days post-STEMI (most commonly after inferior or inferoposterior MI involving posteromedial papillary muscle). Presents with sudden pulmonary edema, new holosystolic murmur, and pulmonary edema on CXR. Clinical pearl: "Post-MI murmur" — Three causes: papillary muscle rupture (urgent surgery), VSD (thrill at LSB), and free wall rupture (PEA arrest). Distinguish by echo.
VSR presents with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the LEFT LOWER STERNAL BORDER with a palpable thrill. The murmur here is apical radiating to axilla, more consistent with MR than VSR.
Free wall rupture presents with sudden electromechanical dissociation (PEA arrest) and hemopericardium. It is rapidly fatal without emergent pericardiocentesis and surgical repair.
Stent thrombosis presents with recurrent chest pain and ST elevation. It would not cause a new murmur or pulmonary edema without extensive LV dysfunction.

rationale: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2-7 days post-STEMI (most commonly after inferior or inferoposterior MI involving posteromedial papillary muscle). Presents with sudden pulmonary edema, new holosystolic murmur, and pulmonary edema on CXR.

question: A 65-year-old with HTN and DM. Echo shows LVH with septal thickness 65 mm, LVOT gradient 65 mmHg at rest, SAM of mitral valve. What is the first-line therapy?

options.rationale: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with LVOT obstruction is treated first-line with beta-blockers. They reduce heart rate, increase diastolic filling time, and decrease contractility → decreased LVOT gradient. Clinical pearl: "HOCM management" — BB first, verapamil second (caution in severe obstruction), disopyramide third. AVOID nitrates, diuretics, digoxin, and inotropes (worsen obstruction).
Dihydropyridine CCBs (nifedipine, amlodipine) are VASODILATORS and can worsen LVOT obstruction by reducing afterload and increasing the gradient. They are avoided in HOCM.
ACE inhibitors reduce afterload, which can worsen LVOT obstruction. Additionally, vasodilation in a hypertrophied ventricle can cause hypotension.
Nitrates reduce preload, decreasing LV cavity size and worsening LVOT obstruction. They are contraindicated in HOCM.

rationale: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with LVOT obstruction is treated first-line with beta-blockers. They reduce heart rate, increase diastolic filling time, and decrease contractility → decreased LVOT gradient.

question: A 68-year-old female with fever, weight loss, and a new diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. He has a history of IV drug use. TEE shows a 68.68 cm vegetation on the aortic valve. What is the most appropriate antibiotics?

options.rationale: IV drug users with native valve endocarditis most commonly have S. aureus (often MRSA). Vancomycin-based regimen is appropriate until sensitivities return. Clinical pearl: "IE in IVDU" — S. aureus is the most common organism (especially tricuspid valve), but left-sided IE in IVDU is also often staph and requires aggressive surgical evaluation.
Enterococcal IE is more common in elderly patients with GI/GU instrumentation, not IV drug users. Ampicillin/gentamicin would not cover the likely staphylococcal infection.
Ceftriaxone covers penicillin-sensitive viridans group streptococci and HACEK organisms. It does NOT adequately cover S. aureus, especially MRSA, which is the primary concern in IV drug users.
Doxycycline is not first-line for any form of IE. It may have some activity against certain organisms but is not bactericidal enough for the high bacterial load seen in IE vegetations.

rationale: IV drug users with native valve endocarditis most commonly have S. aureus (often MRSA).

question: A 70-year-old with STEMI of the anterior wall. Door-to-balloon time 70 min. Post-PCI LVEF 70%. What is the most important medication for mortality reduction in this patient?

options.rationale: In post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40%, spironolactone (eplerenone preferred post-MI) reduces mortality. The EPHESUS trial showed eplerenone reduced all-cause mortality by 15% in post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40% and either HF symptoms or diabetes. Clinical pearl: "Post-MI GDMT" — aspirin + P2Y12i + statin + beta-blocker + ACEi/ARB + MRA (if EF ≤40%).
Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) are contraindicated post-MI with LV dysfunction due to negative inotropic effects. They INCREASE mortality in this population.
Class Ic antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) INCREASE mortality post-MI (CAST trial). They are contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease.
Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but does NOT reduce post-MI mortality (DIG trial). It is reserved for rate control in AF or as add-on in refractory HF.

rationale: In post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40%, spironolactone (eplerenone preferred post-MI) reduces mortality. The EPHESUS trial showed eplerenone reduced all-cause mortality by 15% in post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40% and either HF symptoms or diabetes.

question: A 42-year-old female with chest pain for 42 hours. ECG shows ST depression in V42-V42 with elevated troponin (42.42 ng/mL). What is the diagnosis?

options.rationale: NSTEMI presents with ST depression and elevated troponin. Per 2023 AHA/ACC guidelines, early invasive strategy (angiography within 24h) is indicated for NSTEMI. Clinical pearl: "Troponin defines MI, ECG defines type" — ST depression = NSTEMI, ST elevation = STEMI.
STEMI requires ST elevation in contiguous leads (≥1 mm in limb leads, ≥2 mm in precordial leads). ST depression alone, even with chest pain and positive troponin, defines NSTEMI.
Unstable angina presents with chest pain at rest or with minimal exertion but WITHOUT elevated troponin. Elevated troponin indicates myocardial necrosis, making this an MI.
Pericarditis typically causes diffuse ST elevation (concave upward) with PR depression. It presents with positional chest pain improved by leaning forward, not with elevated troponin to this degree.

rationale: NSTEMI presents with ST depression and elevated troponin. Per 2023 AHA/ACC guidelines, early invasive strategy (angiography within 24h) is indicated for NSTEMI.

question: A 38-year-old male with dyspnea, orthopnea, PND. LVEF 38%. BP 38/38. Cr 38.38. K+ 38.38. What is first-line GDMT?

options.rationale: Per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, HFrEF GDMT is ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA. PARADIGM-HF showed ARNI reduces CV death/HF hospitalization by 20% vs enalapril. Clinical pearl: "GDMT quadruple" — ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i is now the standard for HFrEF.
This is antihypertensive therapy, not HFrEF GDMT. Amlodipine does NOT reduce mortality in heart failure (PRAISE trial). Hypertension management is adjunctive to heart failure therapy.
Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but not mortality (DIG trial). Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not affect disease progression. Neither addresses the neurohormonal cascade driving HF.

Metoprolol tartrate is short-acting; metoprolol succinate (extended-release) is the evidence-based formulation. Nitrates have no mortality benefit in HFrEF (except hydralazine/nitrate combo in African Americans).

rationale: Per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, HFrEF GDMT is ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA. PARADIGM-HF showed ARNI reduces CV death/HF hospitalization by 20% vs enalapril.

question: A 35-year-old female with palpitations, syncope. ECG: irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves, ventricular rate 35 bpm. BP 35/35. What is the appropriate management?

options.rationale: Hemodynamically unstable AF with rapid ventricular response requires immediate synchronized cardioversion per ACLS protocols. Clinical pearl: "Unstable AF = cardiovert" — hypotension, chest pain, or altered mental status with tachyarrhythmia requires immediate electrical therapy, not rate control.

Rate control is appropriate for STABLE AF. This patient is hypotensive (BP 85/50), indicating hemodynamic instability from the rapid rate. Rate control medications take 5-15 minutes to work and may not restore perfusion.
Adenosine is used for narrow-complex SVT (AV nodal reentrant tachycardia), not AF. Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction but AF recurs as adenosine is rapidly cleared (half-life <10 seconds).
IV amiodarone can chemically cardiovert AF but takes hours to work. In unstable patients, electrical cardioversion achieves immediate restoration of sinus rhythm with a single shock.

rationale: Hemodynamically unstable AF with rapid ventricular response requires immediate synchronized cardioversion per ACLS protocols. Clinical pearl: "Unstable AF = cardiovert" — hypotension, chest pain, or altered mental status with tachyarrhythmia requires immediate electrical therapy, not rate control..

question: A 48-year-old diabetic presents with dyspnea and orthopnea. BP 48/48 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows AV nicking and silver-wiring. Cr 48.48. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Hypertensive emergency with acute heart failure
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 with end-organ damage) causing acute pulmonary edema requires rapid BP reduction by 25% over 1 hour with IV nitroprusside or nicardipine. Clinical pearl: "Hypertensive emergency" — do NOT lower BP to normal in first hour; 25% reduction prevents end-organ hypoperfusion.
Valvular regurgitation causes heart failure but does not cause BP 200/120 or the fundoscopic changes described (AV nicking, silver-wiring are chronic hypertensive retinopathy signs).
Takotsubo (stress cardiomyopathy) presents with LV apical ballooning triggered by emotional stress. It mimics STEMI but does not present with acute hypertension or retinopathy.

options.text: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2-7 days post-STEMI causing acute severe MR. No history of recent MI or the fundoscopic findings of chronic hypertension make this less likely.

rationale: Hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 with end-organ damage) causing acute pulmonary edema requires rapid BP reduction by 25% over 1 hour with IV nitroprusside or nicardipine. Clinical pearl: "Hypertensive emergency" — do NOT lower BP to normal in first hour; 25% reduction prevents end-organ hypoperfusion..

question: A 52-year-old with aortic stenosis (aortic valve area 52.52 cm², mean gradient 52 mmHg). Asymptomatic. EF 52%. What is management?

options.text: Clinical surveillance with echo every 6-12 months
options.rationale: Severe AS (AVA <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient with normal EF is managed with close surveillance. AVR is indicated once symptoms develop (dyspnea, angina, syncope) OR EF <50%. Clinical pearl: "AS symptom triad" — angina, syncope, dyspnea. Once symptoms appear, mean survival is 2-3 years without AVR.
AVR is indicated for SYMPTOMATIC severe AS or asymptomatic severe AS with EF <50%. This patient is asymptomatic with normal EF, so watchful waiting is appropriate.
Balloon valvuloplasty has high restenosis rates (50% at 6 months) and is reserved as a bridge to AVR in hemodynamically unstable patients or palliative cases.
No medical therapy improves outcomes in severe AS. Vasodilators are relatively contraindicated as they can cause hypotension (fixed cardiac output from the stenotic valve cannot increase).

rationale: Severe AS (AVA <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient with normal EF is managed with close surveillance. AVR is indicated once symptoms develop (dyspnea, angina, syncope) OR EF <50%.

question: A 55-year-old with HTN, DM, CKD stage 55 presents with BP 55/55. On lisinopril 55 mg, amlodipine 55 mg, HCTZ 55 mg. What is the next step?

options.rationale: Three-drug therapy (ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide) at optimal doses failing to control BP requires a fourth agent. In patients with CKD, resistant HTN, or diabetes, spironolactone is effective. Clinical pearl: "Resistant HTN" — defined as BP above goal despite 3 optimal-dose antihypertensives including a diuretic. Rule out secondary causes and pseudo-resistance.

Beta-blockers are not first-line add-on therapy in uncomplicated resistant HTN (except in specific indications like CAD, HF, or tachycardia). Spironolactone showed superior BP reduction in the PATHWAY-2 trial.

HCTZ 25 mg provides maximum antihypertensive effect; increasing to 50 mg adds minimal BP reduction with more electrolyte disturbances. A thiazide-like diuretic (chlorthalidone 12.5 mg) is more potent.

options.text: Stop lisinopril and start losartan 50 mg
options.rationale: Switching within the same drug class (ACEi to ARB) provides no additional BP reduction. The patient needs a fourth agent, not a substitution of existing therapy.

rationale: Three-drug therapy (ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide) at optimal doses failing to control BP requires a fourth agent. In patients with CKD, resistant HTN, or diabetes, spironolactone is effective.

question: A 58-year-old with acute chest pain. ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF. HR 58, BP 58/58. What is the next step?

options.text: IV fluids + atropine + urgent primary PCI
options.rationale: Inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension suggests RV infarction (ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic). First-line: IV fluids for preload (RV depends on preload), atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, then urgent PCI. Clinical pearl: "RV infarct" — NEVER give nitrates or diuretics in RV infarct; the RV is preload-dependent and these cause catastrophic hypotension.
Beta-blockers are relatively contraindicated in RV infarction. The bradycardia and hypotension indicate the RV is compensating; beta-blockers would worsen both, potentially causing cardiac arrest.
Nitrates cause venodilation reducing RV preload → catastrophic hypotension in RV infarction. Nitrates are contraindicated until RV involvement is excluded.
Diuretics reduce preload and would worsen shock in RV infarction. Furosemide is for LV failure with pulmonary congestion, not for the systemic congestion seen in RV failure.

rationale: Inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension suggests RV infarction (ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic). First-line: IV fluids for preload (RV depends on preload), atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, then urgent PCI.

question: A 60-year-old with syncope. ECG: sinus bradycardia 60 bpm, prolonged QT (QTc 60 ms). K+ 60.60, Mg 60.60. What is the appropriate management?

options.text: IV MgSO4 2g + K+ replacement + stop QT-prolonging drugs
options.rationale: Torsades de pointes risk is high with QTc >500 ms, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia. IV MgSO4 is first-line regardless of serum Mg level. Clinical pearl: "Torsades protocol" — IV MgSO4 2g over 1-2 min, correct K+ to 4.5-5.0, correct Mg >2.0. Isoproterenol or pacing if refractory.
Pacing is reserved for tachy-brady syndrome or when QT-prolonging factors cannot be corrected. Medical management of the reversible causes (K+, Mg, offending drugs) should be attempted first.
Amiodarone PROLONGS the QT interval and predisposes to torsades. It is used for VT/VF arrest but is relatively contraindicated in congenital or acquired long QT syndrome.
Atropine may increase heart rate but does not address the underlying cause of the prolonged QT and does not prevent torsades. The metabolic and pharmacologic triggers must be corrected.

rationale: Torsades de pointes risk is high with QTc >500 ms, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia. IV MgSO4 is first-line regardless of serum Mg level.

question: A 62-year-old with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP right arm 62/62, left arm 62/62. CXR shows widened mediastinum. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.rationale: Aortic dissection presents with tearing chest pain radiating to back with pulse/blood pressure differential. CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice (>95% sensitivity). Clinical pearl: "Aortic dissection mimickers" — STEMI, PE, and MSK pain. Always check BP in both arms and CXR for widened mediastinum.

TTE has poor sensitivity (~60%) for aortic dissection. TEE is better (>90%) but requires esophageal intubation. CT angiography is faster, non-invasive, and provides detail needed for surgical planning (Stanford classification).
While ACS should be considered, the tearing quality, BP differential, and widened mediastinum point strongly toward dissection. CT should not be delayed for ACS rule-out.

Anticoagulation is CONTRAINDICATED until dissection is ruled out. Heparin in dissection would worsen bleeding and increase mortality. If dissection is confirmed, emergency surgical consultation is needed (Type A) or medical management (Type B).

rationale: Aortic dissection presents with tearing chest pain radiating to back with pulse/blood pressure differential. CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice (>95% sensitivity).

question: A 65-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 65%), on optimal GDMT. Still NYHA III. QRS 65 ms, LBBB. What is the next appropriate therapy?

options.rationale: CRT is indicated for HFrEF with LVEF ≤35%, LBBB ≥150 ms, and persistent symptoms despite GDMT. CRT improves mortality, reduces HF hospitalizations, and can reverse remodel the LV. Clinical pearl: "CRT criteria" — EF ≤35%, LBBB ≥150 ms, NYHA II-IV, optimal GDMT. Wider QRS = greater CRT benefit.
While uptitration of GDMT is always considered, the phrase "optimal GDMT" implies this has been maximized. CRT is the next indicated therapy per guidelines.
Transplant evaluation is for advanced HF (NYHA III-IV) despite ALL other therapies including CRT. CRT should be trialed first as it can improve EF and symptoms significantly.
ICD is indicated for primary prevention (EF ≤35%) but this patient has LBBB ≥150 ms, making CRT-D (combined CRT + ICD) superior to ICD alone. CRT improves the underlying mechanical dyssynchrony.

rationale: CRT is indicated for HFrEF with LVEF ≤35%, LBBB ≥150 ms, and persistent symptoms despite GDMT. CRT improves mortality, reduces HF hospitalizations, and can reverse remodel the LV.

question: A 68-year-old female presents with acute-onset dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain 68 days post-C-section. HR 68, BP 68/68, O68 sat 68%. D-dimer 68.68 mg/L. CTPA shows saddle PE. What is the immediate management?

options.rationale: Massive PE (saddle, with hypotension/O2 desat) requires immediate anticoagulation. UFH is preferred due to reversibility (protamine) if thrombolysis or embolectomy is needed. Clinical pearl: "Massive PE management" — UFH + consider systemic thrombolysis if cardiac arrest/obstructive shock. In post-C-section, balancing bleeding risk vs clot burden.

Thrombolysis is indicated for massive PE with obstructive shock or cardiac arrest. This patient has hypotension but not refractory shock. Recent surgery (C-section 5 days ago) increases bleeding risk. Thrombolysis should be reserved for deterioration.
LMWH is appropriate for non-massive PE. In massive PE with hypotension, IV UFH provides more rapid and reversible anticoagulation in case thrombolysis or embolectomy becomes needed.
DOACs are for stable, non-massive PE. In massive PE with hypotension, oral therapy is inappropriate due to unreliable absorption in shock state and lack of reversibility.

rationale: Massive PE (saddle, with hypotension/O2 desat) requires immediate anticoagulation. UFH is preferred due to reversibility (protamine) if thrombolysis or embolectomy is needed.

question: A 70-year-old diabetic presents with atypical chest pain (burning epigastric). ECG non-diagnostic. Troponin 70.70 ng/mL (normal <70.70). What is the most appropriate next step?

options.rationale: Diabetics often present with atypical ("silent") ischemia due to autonomic neuropathy. Elevated troponin with atypical symptoms in a diabetic with risk factors warrants coronary angiography. Clinical pearl: "Silent ischemia in diabetes" — autonomic neuropathy blunts cardiac pain signaling. Any troponin elevation in a diabetic with CAD risk factors should be investigated.

Coronary calcium scoring is for risk stratification in asymptomatic patients. This patient has symptoms (though atypical) AND elevated troponin, making invasive angiography appropriate for diagnosis and possible intervention.

Stress testing is appropriate for intermediate-risk patients with NSTEMI who are pain-free and hemodynamically stable. However, ongoing troponin elevation favors early invasive strategy per guidelines.
While symptoms are atypical, the elevated troponin is objective evidence of myocardial injury. Attributing atypical chest pain to GERD in a diabetic with elevated troponin would miss the diagnosis.

rationale: Diabetics often present with atypical ("silent") ischemia due to autonomic neuropathy. Elevated troponin with atypical symptoms in a diabetic with risk factors warrants coronary angiography.

question: A 72-year-old with dyspnea. Echocardiogram shows LVEF 72%, E/e' ratio 72, left atrial enlargement, LVH. NT-proBNP 72 pg/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
options.rationale: HFpEF is diagnosed with (1) symptoms/signs of HF, (2) LVEF ≥50%, (3) objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction (E/e' >14, LA enlargement, LVH, elevated NT-proBNP). Clinical pearl: "HFA-PEFF algorithm" — use a stepwise approach to diagnose HFpEF: (1) Suspect, (2) Echo/BNP, (3) Stress or invasive testing, (4) Final diagnosis.

Constrictive pericarditis presents with Kussmaul sign, pericardial calcification, and septal bounce on echo. E/e' ratio is typically normal (constriction restricts ALL filling, unlike HFpEF which impairs early relaxation).

PAH presents with right heart strain, not left heart abnormalities. E/e' ratio (marker of LV filling pressure) is normal in PAH. This patient has LVH and LA enlargement suggesting left-sided heart disease.

Cardiac amyloidosis causes LVH with low voltage on ECG (discordance), granular sparkling on echo, and restrictive physiology. While this is a cause of HFpEF, the echo findings here are more consistent with hypertensive heart disease.

rationale: HFpEF is diagnosed with (1) symptoms/signs of HF, (2) LVEF ≥50%, (3) objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction (E/e' >14, LA enlargement, LVH, elevated NT-proBNP). Clinical pearl: "HFA-PEFF algorithm" — use a stepwise approach to diagnose HFpEF: (1) Suspect, (2) Echo/BNP, (3) Stress or invasive testing, (4) Final diagnosis..

question: A 45-year-old presents with palpitations, lightheadedness. ECG shows narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 45 bpm, no visible P waves. BP 45/45. Carotid sinus massage terminates the rhythm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: AVNRT presents with regular narrow-complex tachycardia, no P waves (or retrograde P buried in QRS), and responds to vagal maneuvers/adenosine. It is the most common SVT. Clinical pearl: "SVT response to adenosine" — if it terminates with adenosine, it's AVNRT or AVRT (accessory pathway). If AF/AFlutter persists with AV block, it's atrial in origin.
AF is irregularly irregular, not regular. Carotid sinus massage may slow the ventricular rate but does not terminate AF, as AF is an atrial rhythm independent of AV node function.

Atrial flutter with 2:1 block produces a regular rate of ~150 bpm with visible flutter waves (sawtooth pattern), especially in II, III, aVF. Carotid massage increases block to 3:1 or 4:1, slowing but not terminating the rhythm.
VT is wide-complex (>120 ms). This patient has narrow-complex tachycardia, making SVT the diagnosis. Always assume wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.

rationale: AVNRT presents with regular narrow-complex tachycardia, no P waves (or retrograde P buried in QRS), and responds to vagal maneuvers/adenosine. It is the most common SVT.

question: A 50-year-old with AF on rivaroxaban 50 mg daily. Presents with acute ischemic stroke. What is the management of anticoagulation?

options.text: Hold rivaroxaban, CT head to rule out hemorrhage, start aspirin 81 mg for 24-48h, then re-evaluate
options.rationale: In AF patients on DOAC who have an acute ischemic stroke, guidelines recommend holding anticoagulation, ruling out hemorrhagic conversion with CT, and using aspirin short-term while re-evaluating the risk/benefit of resuming DOAC. Clinical pearl: "AF stroke on DOAC" — check adherence, drug-drug interactions, renal function; consider switching to a different DOAC or warfarin if poor candidate.

Continuing anticoagulation within the first hours of a moderate-to-large acute ischemic stroke risks hemorrhagic conversion (especially if the infarct is large, >1/3 MCA territory). Anticoagulation should be held temporarily.
Switching anticoagulants during acute stroke is not recommended. The priority is neuroimaging to rule out hemorrhage, then short-term aspirin, then re-assess for anticoagulation at day 7-14.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated within 24 hours of DOAC administration. The patient is already on therapeutic anticoagulation, making the risk of hemorrhagic conversion after tPA unacceptably high.

rationale: In AF patients on DOAC who have an acute ischemic stroke, guidelines recommend holding anticoagulation, ruling out hemorrhagic conversion with CT, and using aspirin short-term while re-evaluating the risk/benefit of resuming DOAC. Clinical pearl: "AF stroke on DOAC" — check adherence, drug-drug interactions, renal function; consider switching to a different DOAC or warfarin if poor candidate..

question: A 42-year-old with acute pericarditis. Chest pain worse supine, improved sitting forward. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: High-dose ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID + colchicine 0.5 mg BID
options.rationale: Per 2015 ESC guidelines, first-line therapy for acute pericarditis is NSAIDs (ibuprofen or aspirin) plus colchicine. Colchicine reduces recurrence risk (COPE trial: 32% → 11%). Clinical pearl: "Pericarditis therapy" — NSAID + colchicine for 3 months. Corticosteroids only if refractory or contraindication to NSAIDs (corticosteroids actually increase recurrence risk).

Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory pericarditis, rheumatologic causes, or contraindications to NSAIDs/colchicine. The IMPI study showed corticosteroids increase recurrence risk by 3x compared to NSAIDs.

Purulent (bacterial) pericarditis is rare and presents with high fever, toxic appearance, and purulent pericardial fluid. Acute pericarditis is most commonly viral or idiopathic and does not require antibiotics.
Low-dose aspirin is antiplatelet, not anti-inflammatory. High-dose aspirin (2-4 g/day) or ibuprofen (600-800 mg TID) is needed to achieve the anti-inflammatory effect required for pericarditis.

rationale: Per 2015 ESC guidelines, first-line therapy for acute pericarditis is NSAIDs (ibuprofen or aspirin) plus colchicine. Colchicine reduces recurrence risk (COPE trial: 32% → 11%).

question: A 38-year-old with acute-onset palpitations. ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia (38 bpm). BP 38/38. IV adenosine 38 mg converts to sinus rhythm. What is the diagnosis?

options.rationale: Adenosine-sensitive narrow-complex tachycardia that abruptly terminates is diagnostic of AVNRT or AVRT involving the AV node as part of the reentrant circuit. Clinical pearl: "Adenosine effect" — If tachycardia terminates, the AV node was part of the circuit (AVNRT/AVRT/WPW). If AF with block appears, the atrium is the source.
Atrial flutter does not typically terminate with adenosine; adenosine increases AV block, revealing the flutter waves without terminating the atrial rhythm.
Focal atrial tachycardia may or may not terminate with adenosine (depends on mechanism: triggered vs reentrant). However, AVNRT is far more common and the response to adenosine is classic.
VT is wide-complex. Narrow-complex tachycardia (QRS <120 ms) originates above the ventricles, defining it as SVT.

rationale: Adenosine-sensitive narrow-complex tachycardia that abruptly terminates is diagnostic of AVNRT or AVRT involving the AV node as part of the reentrant circuit. Clinical pearl: "Adenosine effect" — If tachycardia terminates, the AV node was part of the circuit (AVNRT/AVRT/WPW).

question: A 35-year-old with STEMI undergoes primary PCI to the LAD. Post-procedure day 35, develops sudden dyspnea and hypoxia. New pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla. CXR shows pulmonary edema. What is the most likely complication?

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2-7 days post-STEMI (most commonly after inferior or inferoposterior MI involving posteromedial papillary muscle). Presents with sudden pulmonary edema, new holosystolic murmur, and pulmonary edema on CXR. Clinical pearl: "Post-MI murmur" — Three causes: papillary muscle rupture (urgent surgery), VSD (thrill at LSB), and free wall rupture (PEA arrest). Distinguish by echo.
VSR presents with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the LEFT LOWER STERNAL BORDER with a palpable thrill. The murmur here is apical radiating to axilla, more consistent with MR than VSR.
Free wall rupture presents with sudden electromechanical dissociation (PEA arrest) and hemopericardium. It is rapidly fatal without emergent pericardiocentesis and surgical repair.
Stent thrombosis presents with recurrent chest pain and ST elevation. It would not cause a new murmur or pulmonary edema without extensive LV dysfunction.

rationale: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2-7 days post-STEMI (most commonly after inferior or inferoposterior MI involving posteromedial papillary muscle). Presents with sudden pulmonary edema, new holosystolic murmur, and pulmonary edema on CXR.

question: A 48-year-old with HTN and DM. Echo shows LVH with septal thickness 48 mm, LVOT gradient 48 mmHg at rest, SAM of mitral valve. What is the first-line therapy?

options.rationale: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with LVOT obstruction is treated first-line with beta-blockers. They reduce heart rate, increase diastolic filling time, and decrease contractility → decreased LVOT gradient. Clinical pearl: "HOCM management" — BB first, verapamil second (caution in severe obstruction), disopyramide third. AVOID nitrates, diuretics, digoxin, and inotropes (worsen obstruction).
Dihydropyridine CCBs (nifedipine, amlodipine) are VASODILATORS and can worsen LVOT obstruction by reducing afterload and increasing the gradient. They are avoided in HOCM.
ACE inhibitors reduce afterload, which can worsen LVOT obstruction. Additionally, vasodilation in a hypertrophied ventricle can cause hypotension.
Nitrates reduce preload, decreasing LV cavity size and worsening LVOT obstruction. They are contraindicated in HOCM.

rationale: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) with LVOT obstruction is treated first-line with beta-blockers. They reduce heart rate, increase diastolic filling time, and decrease contractility → decreased LVOT gradient.

question: A 52-year-old male with fever, weight loss, and a new diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. He has a history of IV drug use. TEE shows a 52.52 cm vegetation on the aortic valve. What is the most appropriate antibiotics?

options.rationale: IV drug users with native valve endocarditis most commonly have S. aureus (often MRSA). Vancomycin-based regimen is appropriate until sensitivities return. Clinical pearl: "IE in IVDU" — S. aureus is the most common organism (especially tricuspid valve), but left-sided IE in IVDU is also often staph and requires aggressive surgical evaluation.
Enterococcal IE is more common in elderly patients with GI/GU instrumentation, not IV drug users. Ampicillin/gentamicin would not cover the likely staphylococcal infection.
Ceftriaxone covers penicillin-sensitive viridans group streptococci and HACEK organisms. It does NOT adequately cover S. aureus, especially MRSA, which is the primary concern in IV drug users.
Doxycycline is not first-line for any form of IE. It may have some activity against certain organisms but is not bactericidal enough for the high bacterial load seen in IE vegetations.

rationale: IV drug users with native valve endocarditis most commonly have S. aureus (often MRSA).

question: A 55-year-old with STEMI of the anterior wall. Door-to-balloon time 55 min. Post-PCI LVEF 55%. What is the most important medication for mortality reduction in this patient?

options.rationale: In post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40%, spironolactone (eplerenone preferred post-MI) reduces mortality. The EPHESUS trial showed eplerenone reduced all-cause mortality by 15% in post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40% and either HF symptoms or diabetes. Clinical pearl: "Post-MI GDMT" — aspirin + P2Y12i + statin + beta-blocker + ACEi/ARB + MRA (if EF ≤40%).
Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) are contraindicated post-MI with LV dysfunction due to negative inotropic effects. They INCREASE mortality in this population.
Class Ic antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) INCREASE mortality post-MI (CAST trial). They are contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease.
Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but does NOT reduce post-MI mortality (DIG trial). It is reserved for rate control in AF or as add-on in refractory HF.

rationale: In post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40%, spironolactone (eplerenone preferred post-MI) reduces mortality. The EPHESUS trial showed eplerenone reduced all-cause mortality by 15% in post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40% and either HF symptoms or diabetes.

question: A 65-year-old male with chest pain for 65 hours. ECG shows ST depression in V65-V65 with elevated troponin (65.65 ng/mL). What is the diagnosis?

options.rationale: NSTEMI presents with ST depression and elevated troponin. Per 2023 AHA/ACC guidelines, early invasive strategy (angiography within 24h) is indicated for NSTEMI. Clinical pearl: "Troponin defines MI, ECG defines type" — ST depression = NSTEMI, ST elevation = STEMI.
STEMI requires ST elevation in contiguous leads (≥1 mm in limb leads, ≥2 mm in precordial leads). ST depression alone, even with chest pain and positive troponin, defines NSTEMI.
Unstable angina presents with chest pain at rest or with minimal exertion but WITHOUT elevated troponin. Elevated troponin indicates myocardial necrosis, making this an MI.
Pericarditis typically causes diffuse ST elevation (concave upward) with PR depression. It presents with positional chest pain improved by leaning forward, not with elevated troponin to this degree.

rationale: NSTEMI presents with ST depression and elevated troponin. Per 2023 AHA/ACC guidelines, early invasive strategy (angiography within 24h) is indicated for NSTEMI.

question: A 68-year-old female with dyspnea, orthopnea, PND. LVEF 68%. BP 68/68. Cr 68.68. K+ 68.68. What is first-line GDMT?

options.rationale: Per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, HFrEF GDMT is ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA. PARADIGM-HF showed ARNI reduces CV death/HF hospitalization by 20% vs enalapril. Clinical pearl: "GDMT quadruple" — ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i is now the standard for HFrEF.
This is antihypertensive therapy, not HFrEF GDMT. Amlodipine does NOT reduce mortality in heart failure (PRAISE trial). Hypertension management is adjunctive to heart failure therapy.
Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but not mortality (DIG trial). Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not affect disease progression. Neither addresses the neurohormonal cascade driving HF.

Metoprolol tartrate is short-acting; metoprolol succinate (extended-release) is the evidence-based formulation. Nitrates have no mortality benefit in HFrEF (except hydralazine/nitrate combo in African Americans).

rationale: Per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, HFrEF GDMT is ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA. PARADIGM-HF showed ARNI reduces CV death/HF hospitalization by 20% vs enalapril.

question: A 70-year-old male with palpitations, syncope. ECG: irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves, ventricular rate 70 bpm. BP 70/70. What is the appropriate management?

options.rationale: Hemodynamically unstable AF with rapid ventricular response requires immediate synchronized cardioversion per ACLS protocols. Clinical pearl: "Unstable AF = cardiovert" — hypotension, chest pain, or altered mental status with tachyarrhythmia requires immediate electrical therapy, not rate control.

Rate control is appropriate for STABLE AF. This patient is hypotensive (BP 85/50), indicating hemodynamic instability from the rapid rate. Rate control medications take 5-15 minutes to work and may not restore perfusion.
Adenosine is used for narrow-complex SVT (AV nodal reentrant tachycardia), not AF. Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction but AF recurs as adenosine is rapidly cleared (half-life <10 seconds).
IV amiodarone can chemically cardiovert AF but takes hours to work. In unstable patients, electrical cardioversion achieves immediate restoration of sinus rhythm with a single shock.

rationale: Hemodynamically unstable AF with rapid ventricular response requires immediate synchronized cardioversion per ACLS protocols. Clinical pearl: "Unstable AF = cardiovert" — hypotension, chest pain, or altered mental status with tachyarrhythmia requires immediate electrical therapy, not rate control..

question: A 72-year-old diabetic presents with dyspnea and orthopnea. BP 72/72 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows AV nicking and silver-wiring. Cr 72.72. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Hypertensive emergency with acute heart failure
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 with end-organ damage) causing acute pulmonary edema requires rapid BP reduction by 25% over 1 hour with IV nitroprusside or nicardipine. Clinical pearl: "Hypertensive emergency" — do NOT lower BP to normal in first hour; 25% reduction prevents end-organ hypoperfusion.
Valvular regurgitation causes heart failure but does not cause BP 200/120 or the fundoscopic changes described (AV nicking, silver-wiring are chronic hypertensive retinopathy signs).
Takotsubo (stress cardiomyopathy) presents with LV apical ballooning triggered by emotional stress. It mimics STEMI but does not present with acute hypertension or retinopathy.

options.text: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2-7 days post-STEMI causing acute severe MR. No history of recent MI or the fundoscopic findings of chronic hypertension make this less likely.

rationale: Hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 with end-organ damage) causing acute pulmonary edema requires rapid BP reduction by 25% over 1 hour with IV nitroprusside or nicardipine. Clinical pearl: "Hypertensive emergency" — do NOT lower BP to normal in first hour; 25% reduction prevents end-organ hypoperfusion..

question: A 45-year-old with aortic stenosis (aortic valve area 45.45 cm², mean gradient 45 mmHg). Asymptomatic. EF 45%. What is management?

options.text: Clinical surveillance with echo every 6-12 months
options.rationale: Severe AS (AVA <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient with normal EF is managed with close surveillance. AVR is indicated once symptoms develop (dyspnea, angina, syncope) OR EF <50%. Clinical pearl: "AS symptom triad" — angina, syncope, dyspnea. Once symptoms appear, mean survival is 2-3 years without AVR.
AVR is indicated for SYMPTOMATIC severe AS or asymptomatic severe AS with EF <50%. This patient is asymptomatic with normal EF, so watchful waiting is appropriate.
Balloon valvuloplasty has high restenosis rates (50% at 6 months) and is reserved as a bridge to AVR in hemodynamically unstable patients or palliative cases.
No medical therapy improves outcomes in severe AS. Vasodilators are relatively contraindicated as they can cause hypotension (fixed cardiac output from the stenotic valve cannot increase).

rationale: Severe AS (AVA <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient with normal EF is managed with close surveillance. AVR is indicated once symptoms develop (dyspnea, angina, syncope) OR EF <50%.

question: A 50-year-old with HTN, DM, CKD stage 50 presents with BP 50/50. On lisinopril 50 mg, amlodipine 50 mg, HCTZ 50 mg. What is the next step?

options.rationale: Three-drug therapy (ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide) at optimal doses failing to control BP requires a fourth agent. In patients with CKD, resistant HTN, or diabetes, spironolactone is effective. Clinical pearl: "Resistant HTN" — defined as BP above goal despite 3 optimal-dose antihypertensives including a diuretic. Rule out secondary causes and pseudo-resistance.

Beta-blockers are not first-line add-on therapy in uncomplicated resistant HTN (except in specific indications like CAD, HF, or tachycardia). Spironolactone showed superior BP reduction in the PATHWAY-2 trial.

HCTZ 25 mg provides maximum antihypertensive effect; increasing to 50 mg adds minimal BP reduction with more electrolyte disturbances. A thiazide-like diuretic (chlorthalidone 12.5 mg) is more potent.

options.text: Stop lisinopril and start losartan 50 mg
options.rationale: Switching within the same drug class (ACEi to ARB) provides no additional BP reduction. The patient needs a fourth agent, not a substitution of existing therapy.

rationale: Three-drug therapy (ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide) at optimal doses failing to control BP requires a fourth agent. In patients with CKD, resistant HTN, or diabetes, spironolactone is effective.

question: A 42-year-old with acute chest pain. ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF. HR 42, BP 42/42. What is the next step?

options.text: IV fluids + atropine + urgent primary PCI
options.rationale: Inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension suggests RV infarction (ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic). First-line: IV fluids for preload (RV depends on preload), atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, then urgent PCI. Clinical pearl: "RV infarct" — NEVER give nitrates or diuretics in RV infarct; the RV is preload-dependent and these cause catastrophic hypotension.
Beta-blockers are relatively contraindicated in RV infarction. The bradycardia and hypotension indicate the RV is compensating; beta-blockers would worsen both, potentially causing cardiac arrest.
Nitrates cause venodilation reducing RV preload → catastrophic hypotension in RV infarction. Nitrates are contraindicated until RV involvement is excluded.
Diuretics reduce preload and would worsen shock in RV infarction. Furosemide is for LV failure with pulmonary congestion, not for the systemic congestion seen in RV failure.

rationale: Inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension suggests RV infarction (ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic). First-line: IV fluids for preload (RV depends on preload), atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, then urgent PCI.

question: A 38-year-old with syncope. ECG: sinus bradycardia 38 bpm, prolonged QT (QTc 38 ms). K+ 38.38, Mg 38.38. What is the appropriate management?

options.text: IV MgSO4 2g + K+ replacement + stop QT-prolonging drugs
options.rationale: Torsades de pointes risk is high with QTc >500 ms, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia. IV MgSO4 is first-line regardless of serum Mg level. Clinical pearl: "Torsades protocol" — IV MgSO4 2g over 1-2 min, correct K+ to 4.5-5.0, correct Mg >2.0. Isoproterenol or pacing if refractory.
Pacing is reserved for tachy-brady syndrome or when QT-prolonging factors cannot be corrected. Medical management of the reversible causes (K+, Mg, offending drugs) should be attempted first.
Amiodarone PROLONGS the QT interval and predisposes to torsades. It is used for VT/VF arrest but is relatively contraindicated in congenital or acquired long QT syndrome.
Atropine may increase heart rate but does not address the underlying cause of the prolonged QT and does not prevent torsades. The metabolic and pharmacologic triggers must be corrected.

rationale: Torsades de pointes risk is high with QTc >500 ms, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia. IV MgSO4 is first-line regardless of serum Mg level.

question: A 35-year-old with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP right arm 35/35, left arm 35/35. CXR shows widened mediastinum. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.rationale: Aortic dissection presents with tearing chest pain radiating to back with pulse/blood pressure differential. CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice (>95% sensitivity). Clinical pearl: "Aortic dissection mimickers" — STEMI, PE, and MSK pain. Always check BP in both arms and CXR for widened mediastinum.

TTE has poor sensitivity (~60%) for aortic dissection. TEE is better (>90%) but requires esophageal intubation. CT angiography is faster, non-invasive, and provides detail needed for surgical planning (Stanford classification).
While ACS should be considered, the tearing quality, BP differential, and widened mediastinum point strongly toward dissection. CT should not be delayed for ACS rule-out.

Anticoagulation is CONTRAINDICATED until dissection is ruled out. Heparin in dissection would worsen bleeding and increase mortality. If dissection is confirmed, emergency surgical consultation is needed (Type A) or medical management (Type B).

rationale: Aortic dissection presents with tearing chest pain radiating to back with pulse/blood pressure differential. CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice (>95% sensitivity).

question: A 48-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 48%), on optimal GDMT. Still NYHA III. QRS 48 ms, LBBB. What is the next appropriate therapy?

options.rationale: CRT is indicated for HFrEF with LVEF ≤35%, LBBB ≥150 ms, and persistent symptoms despite GDMT. CRT improves mortality, reduces HF hospitalizations, and can reverse remodel the LV. Clinical pearl: "CRT criteria" — EF ≤35%, LBBB ≥150 ms, NYHA II-IV, optimal GDMT. Wider QRS = greater CRT benefit.
While uptitration of GDMT is always considered, the phrase "optimal GDMT" implies this has been maximized. CRT is the next indicated therapy per guidelines.
Transplant evaluation is for advanced HF (NYHA III-IV) despite ALL other therapies including CRT. CRT should be trialed first as it can improve EF and symptoms significantly.
ICD is indicated for primary prevention (EF ≤35%) but this patient has LBBB ≥150 ms, making CRT-D (combined CRT + ICD) superior to ICD alone. CRT improves the underlying mechanical dyssynchrony.

rationale: CRT is indicated for HFrEF with LVEF ≤35%, LBBB ≥150 ms, and persistent symptoms despite GDMT. CRT improves mortality, reduces HF hospitalizations, and can reverse remodel the LV.

question: A 52-year-old male presents with acute-onset dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain 52 days post-C-section. HR 52, BP 52/52, O52 sat 52%. D-dimer 52.52 mg/L. CTPA shows saddle PE. What is the immediate management?

options.rationale: Massive PE (saddle, with hypotension/O2 desat) requires immediate anticoagulation. UFH is preferred due to reversibility (protamine) if thrombolysis or embolectomy is needed. Clinical pearl: "Massive PE management" — UFH + consider systemic thrombolysis if cardiac arrest/obstructive shock. In post-C-section, balancing bleeding risk vs clot burden.

Thrombolysis is indicated for massive PE with obstructive shock or cardiac arrest. This patient has hypotension but not refractory shock. Recent surgery (C-section 5 days ago) increases bleeding risk. Thrombolysis should be reserved for deterioration.
LMWH is appropriate for non-massive PE. In massive PE with hypotension, IV UFH provides more rapid and reversible anticoagulation in case thrombolysis or embolectomy becomes needed.
DOACs are for stable, non-massive PE. In massive PE with hypotension, oral therapy is inappropriate due to unreliable absorption in shock state and lack of reversibility.

rationale: Massive PE (saddle, with hypotension/O2 desat) requires immediate anticoagulation. UFH is preferred due to reversibility (protamine) if thrombolysis or embolectomy is needed.

question: A 55-year-old diabetic presents with atypical chest pain (burning epigastric). ECG non-diagnostic. Troponin 55.55 ng/mL (normal <55.55). What is the most appropriate next step?

options.rationale: Diabetics often present with atypical ("silent") ischemia due to autonomic neuropathy. Elevated troponin with atypical symptoms in a diabetic with risk factors warrants coronary angiography. Clinical pearl: "Silent ischemia in diabetes" — autonomic neuropathy blunts cardiac pain signaling. Any troponin elevation in a diabetic with CAD risk factors should be investigated.

Coronary calcium scoring is for risk stratification in asymptomatic patients. This patient has symptoms (though atypical) AND elevated troponin, making invasive angiography appropriate for diagnosis and possible intervention.

Stress testing is appropriate for intermediate-risk patients with NSTEMI who are pain-free and hemodynamically stable. However, ongoing troponin elevation favors early invasive strategy per guidelines.
While symptoms are atypical, the elevated troponin is objective evidence of myocardial injury. Attributing atypical chest pain to GERD in a diabetic with elevated troponin would miss the diagnosis.

rationale: Diabetics often present with atypical ("silent") ischemia due to autonomic neuropathy. Elevated troponin with atypical symptoms in a diabetic with risk factors warrants coronary angiography.

question: A 58-year-old with dyspnea. Echocardiogram shows LVEF 58%, E/e' ratio 58, left atrial enlargement, LVH. NT-proBNP 58 pg/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
options.rationale: HFpEF is diagnosed with (1) symptoms/signs of HF, (2) LVEF ≥50%, (3) objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction (E/e' >14, LA enlargement, LVH, elevated NT-proBNP). Clinical pearl: "HFA-PEFF algorithm" — use a stepwise approach to diagnose HFpEF: (1) Suspect, (2) Echo/BNP, (3) Stress or invasive testing, (4) Final diagnosis.

Constrictive pericarditis presents with Kussmaul sign, pericardial calcification, and septal bounce on echo. E/e' ratio is typically normal (constriction restricts ALL filling, unlike HFpEF which impairs early relaxation).

PAH presents with right heart strain, not left heart abnormalities. E/e' ratio (marker of LV filling pressure) is normal in PAH. This patient has LVH and LA enlargement suggesting left-sided heart disease.

Cardiac amyloidosis causes LVH with low voltage on ECG (discordance), granular sparkling on echo, and restrictive physiology. While this is a cause of HFpEF, the echo findings here are more consistent with hypertensive heart disease.

rationale: HFpEF is diagnosed with (1) symptoms/signs of HF, (2) LVEF ≥50%, (3) objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction (E/e' >14, LA enlargement, LVH, elevated NT-proBNP). Clinical pearl: "HFA-PEFF algorithm" — use a stepwise approach to diagnose HFpEF: (1) Suspect, (2) Echo/BNP, (3) Stress or invasive testing, (4) Final diagnosis..

question: A 65-year-old with COPD (GOLD 3) presents with increased dyspnea, purulent sputum. ABG: pH 7.28, pCO2 75, pO2 50. HR 110, RR 32, using accessory muscles. After 2 hours of BiPAP, pH 7.24, pCO2 80. What is the next step?

options.rationale: NIPPV failure (worsening hypercapnia and acidosis after 1-2 hours) requires intubation per GOLD 2024 guidelines. Criteria: pH <7.25 despite NIPPV, hemodynamic instability, altered mental status, inability to clear secretions. Clinical pearl: "NIPPV success indicators" — pH improvement and RR reduction within 1-2 hours predict success. Worsening = intubate.

While adjusting BiPAP settings is appropriate, the patient has failed NIPPV (worsening acidosis). Further medical management without intubation risks respiratory arrest. NIPPV failure is defined as no improvement after 1-2 hours.

Respiratory stimulants (doxapram, almitrine) have no role in modern COPD management. They increase O2 consumption and can cause arrhythmias. NIPPV is the standard, and when it fails, intubation is indicated.

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is NOT recommended for respiratory acidosis. It can worsen intracellular acidosis by generating CO2. The treatment is improving ventilation, not buffering the pH.

rationale: NIPPV failure (worsening hypercapnia and acidosis after 1-2 hours) requires intubation per GOLD 2024 guidelines. Criteria: pH <7.25 despite NIPPV, hemodynamic instability, altered mental status, inability to clear secretions.

question: A 28-year-old female presents with acute dyspnea, wheezing, and coughing after exposure to cat dander. PEF 40% predicted. Not improving after 3 rounds of salbutamol nebulizer. What is the most appropriate therapy?

options.rationale: Acute severe asthma not responding to initial bronchodilators requires IV MgSO4. It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and reduces hospitalizations. Clinical pearl: "Asthma step-up" — mild: SABA → moderate: SABA + ipratropium + oral steroids → severe: add IV MgSO4 → imminent: IV salbutamol, helium-oxygen, consider intubation.

Aminophylline is no longer recommended in acute asthma exacerbations (NAEPP 2022 guidelines). It has a narrow therapeutic window, causes arrhythmias and seizures, and adds no benefit to standard therapy.
IV salbutamol is reserved for life-threatening asthma (silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion) not responding to MgSO4. It carries significant cardiac side effects (tachycardia, hypokalemia).
Ipratropium is added to salbutamol in acute exacerbations and has likely already been given. This patient needs escalation to IV therapy after maximum inhaled therapy fails.

rationale: Acute severe asthma not responding to initial bronchodilators requires IV MgSO4. It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and reduces hospitalizations.

question: A 55-year-old with CAP: fever 39°C, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, RR 28, HR 110, BP 95/60. O2 sat 87% on room air. CXR shows left lower lobe consolidation. CURB-65 score 3. What is the most appropriate setting?

options.rationale: CURB-65 ≥3 indicates severe CAP requiring hospital admission. Clinical pearl: "CAP severity" — Use CURB-65 or CRB-65 to guide admission decisions. Score 3-5 = severe, admit to ICU.
CURB-65 3 has ~17% mortality. This patient needs IV antibiotics and close monitoring in the hospital, not outpatient management.

options.text: IV antibiotics on the medical ward
options.rationale: While ward admission is an option for CURB-65 2, this patient has CURB-65 3 with hypoxia (O2 sat 87%) and borderline hypotension, meeting criteria for ICU-level care per IDSA/ATS minor criteria.
CURB-65 3 requires dual antibiotic therapy (beta-lactam + macrolide). Azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate for severe CAP, especially if S. pneumoniae or gram-negative organisms are suspected.

rationale: CURB-65 ≥3 indicates severe CAP requiring hospital admission. IDSA/ATS criteria for severe CAP include: major criteria (septic shock, respiratory failure requiring ventilation) and minor criteria (RR ≥30, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension).

question: A 40-year-old presents with hemoptysis, sinusitis, and nasal crusting. CT shows cavitary lung lesions and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: GPA classically presents with upper respiratory (sinusitis, nasal crusting), lower respiratory (hemoptysis, cavitary nodules), and renal (hematuria, RPGN) involvement. TB presents with apical infiltrates, cavitary lesions, and hemoptysis but does not cause sinusitis or nasal crusting. AFB smear and culture would be positive. Granulomas in TB are caseating, not necrotizing vasculitis.

Sarcoidosis presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, non-caseating granulomas, and pulmonary infiltrates. It does NOT cause cavitary lesions or nasal crusting. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is often elevated.
ABPA occurs in patients with asthma or CF, presenting with pulmonary infiltrates, bronchiectasis, and elevated IgE. It does not cause cavitary lesions, sinusitis, or nasal crusting as seen in GPA.

rationale: GPA classically presents with upper respiratory (sinusitis, nasal crusting), lower respiratory (hemoptysis, cavitary nodules), and renal (hematuria, RPGN) involvement. C-ANCA (anti-PR3) is positive in >90% of cases.

question: A 70-year-old with progressive dyspnea and dry cough for 6 months. Exam: bilateral basilar crackles, clubbing. HRCT shows reticular opacities, honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis in a peripheral, basal distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?

No biopsy needed if HRCT is classic. Clinical pearl: "IPF diagnosis" — HRCT can diagnose IPF without biopsy if classic UIP pattern is present. Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) slow progression.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis presents with centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation, and air trapping on expiratory CT. Upper/mid lung predominance, not basilar. History of antigen exposure (mold, birds) is key.

OP presents with peripheral or peribronchial consolidations (reversed halo sign), not reticular opacities and honeycombing. It responds dramatically to corticosteroids, unlike IPF which progresses despite treatment.

Sarcoidosis has upper/mid lung predominance with perilymphatic nodules and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Honeycombing is not a feature of early sarcoidosis. The basilar, peripheral distribution is classic for UIP.

rationale: UIP pattern on HRCT (reticular opacities, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, peripheral/basal distribution) with clinical presentation of progressive dyspnea in an older adult is diagnostic of IPF. No biopsy needed if HRCT is classic.

question: A 45-year-old with PE (segmental). sPESI 0 (no risk factors). BP 120/80, O2 96%. No RV strain on echo. What is the most appropriate management setting?

options.text: Outpatient management with DOAC (rivaroxaban or apixaban)
options.rationale: sPESI 0 patients have 30-day mortality <1% and are candidates for outpatient PE management. Clinical pearl: "Outpatient PE criteria" — sPESI 0, no hypoxia, no RV strain, no active bleeding, reliable follow-up. Outpatient management reduces costs and improves patient satisfaction.

options.text: IV heparin infusion in the hospital
options.rationale: Hospital admission is required for high-risk (sPESI ≥1) or intermediate-risk PE. This patient is low-risk with sPESI 0 and can be managed at home with direct oral anticoagulation.

options.text: DOAC bridge with LMWH for 5 days
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban and apixaban can be used as monotherapy without LMWH bridge (the initial higher dose provides monotherapy). Dabigatran and edoxaban require 5 days of LMWH before starting.

IVC filters are indicated for patients with contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation. This patient has no contraindication and is a candidate for DOAC therapy.

rationale: sPESI 0 patients have 30-day mortality <1% and are candidates for outpatient PE management. Clinical pearl: "Outpatient PE criteria" — sPESI 0, no hypoxia, no RV strain, no active bleeding, reliable follow-up.

question: A 32-year-old with asthma using SABA 3-4x/week, nocturnal symptoms 2x/week, FEV1 85%. What is the appropriate step-up therapy?

options.text: Low-dose ICS-formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
options.rationale: Per GINA 2023, asthma step 2 treatment is low-dose ICS-formoterol (MART). This replaces the old recommendation of low-dose ICS + PRN SABA. MART reduces exacerbation risk by 30-40% compared to SABA alone. Clinical pearl: "GINA paradigm shift" — ICS-formoterol as both maintenance and reliever is now preferred for steps 2-5. SABA-only is no longer recommended.

High-dose ICS is for step 4-5 asthma. This patient has mild persistent asthma (step 2) where low-dose ICS-formoterol MART is appropriate. High-dose ICS increases risk of adrenal suppression and oral thrush.
Montelukast is an alternative but less effective than low-dose ICS. It is primarily used for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, allergic rhinitis, or in patients who cannot use ICS.

options.text: Continue SABA alone with better trigger avoidance
options.rationale: GINA 2023 no longer recommends SABA-only treatment for ANY step of asthma. SABA-only increases exacerbation risk and mortality. All patients should receive ICS-containing therapy.

rationale: Per GINA 2023, asthma step 2 treatment is low-dose ICS-formoterol (MART). This replaces the old recommendation of low-dose ICS + PRN SABA.

question: A 60-year-old presents with dyspnea and cough. CXR shows a 3 cm solitary pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe. The patient is a 40-pack-year smoker. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT chest with contrast + PET-CT if solid nodule ≥8 mm
options.rationale: Per Fleischner Society guidelines, solid nodules ≥8 mm in high-risk patients warrant PET-CT, bronchoscopy, or CT-guided biopsy, or surveillance at 3 months depending on probability. Clinical pearl: "Solitary pulmonary nodule" — risk factors: age >35, smoking history, nodule size, upper lobe location, spiculated margins. Calculate pretest probability (Brock model or Mayo model).
A 3 cm nodule in a heavy smoker is high-risk. CXR lacks sensitivity for characterization. CT is mandatory for proper evaluation of size, density, margins, and growth rate.
Sputum cytology has low sensitivity (20-40%) for peripheral lung nodules. It is more useful for central/large airway lesions. CT-guided biopsy or bronchoscopy is needed for tissue diagnosis.

options.text: Empiric antibiotics for 2 weeks and repeat CXR
options.rationale: Empiric antibiotics for a non-infectious appearing nodule in a high-risk patient wastes time. A 3 cm nodule is too large for watchful waiting. It requires urgent characterization and possible biopsy.

rationale: Per Fleischner Society guidelines, solid nodules ≥8 mm in high-risk patients warrant PET-CT, bronchoscopy, or CT-guided biopsy, or surveillance at 3 months depending on probability. question: A 50-year-old on chronic steroids for RA presents with fever 39°C, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. CXR shows right upper lobe cavity with air-fluid level. What is the most likely organism?

options.rationale: Immunosuppressed patients (chronic steroids) are at high risk for reactivation TB. Upper lobe cavitary lesion with air-fluid level is classic for post-primary TB. Clinical pearl: "TB reactivation risk" — steroids, TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab), HIV, diabetes, CKD. Always screen for latent TB before starting immunosuppressive therapy.

Klebsiella causes upper lobe consolidation (bulging fissure sign) and can cavitate. However, it typically presents acutely in alcoholic or diabetic patients with purulent sputum, not in the setting of chronic steroid use.

Aspergilloma forms in pre-existing cavities (from TB, sarcoidosis). The patient has a new cavity, not a pre-existing one. Invasive aspergillosis occurs in severely neutropenic patients, not chronic steroid users on mucolytics.

Lung abscess from aspiration presents with a cavity and air-fluid level but typically in the dependent segments (posterior upper lobes, superior lower lobes). It requires risk factors for aspiration (alcoholism, G tube, dysphagia), not stated here.

rationale: Immunosuppressed patients (chronic steroids) are at high risk for reactivation TB. Upper lobe cavitary lesion with air-fluid level is classic for post-primary TB.

question: A 55-year-old with progressive dyspnea. HRCT shows mosaic attenuation, air trapping on expiration, and mild centrilobular emphysema. FEV1/FVC 0.65, FEV1 55%, DLCO 45%, TLC 110%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: COPD with emphysema, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency suspected
options.rationale: COPD with lower-lobe predominant emphysema (centrilobular), low DLCO indicating emphysema, hyperinflation (TLC >100%), and relatively preserved FEV1 for the DLCO suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Clinical pearl: "AAT deficiency" — test in all COPD patients with basilar emphysema, young age (<45), minimal smoking history, or family history. Diagnosed by low AAT level + protease inhibitor genotyping.

Bronchiectasis presents with cough, purulent sputum, and airway dilation on CT. HRCT would show bronchial wall thickening and tram-track opacities, not mosaic attenuation/air trapping as the dominant feature.
LAM presents in premenopausal women with recurrent pneumothorax, chylothorax, and thin-walled cysts on HRCT. This patient is male, ruling out LAM.
Pulmonary LCH presents in young smokers with nodular and cystic lesions in the upper lobes. Centrilobular emphysema and mosaic attenuation are not typical features.

rationale: COPD with lower-lobe predominant emphysema (centrilobular), low DLCO indicating emphysema, hyperinflation (TLC >100%), and relatively preserved FEV1 for the DLCO suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. question: A 25-year-old with sudden onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Decreased breath sounds on the right, tracheal deviation to the left. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate needle decompression - 14G cannula in 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax presents with hypotension, tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side, distended neck veins, and respiratory distress. Needle decompression is life-saving. Clinical pearl: "Tension pneumothorax" — do NOT wait for CXR. Clinical diagnosis. Decompress with 14G cannula in 2nd ICS MCL or 5th ICS anterior axillary line, then place chest tube.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis made by tracheal deviation, hypotension, and absent breath sounds. Delaying treatment for CXR can be fatal as tension physiology progresses rapidly.

options.text: Chest tube placement in triangle of safety
options.rationale: Chest tube placement is definitive therapy but takes preparation and time. Immediate needle decompression is the first step to relieve pressure, followed by chest tube placement.
Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency requiring immediate decompression. Oxygen and observation have no role in the acute management.

rationale: Tension pneumothorax presents with hypotension, tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side, distended neck veins, and respiratory distress. Needle decompression is life-saving.

question: A 48-year-old with bilateral pleural effusions. Thoracentesis: exudative (Light's criteria). Cytology negative for malignancy. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

options.rationale: CT chest is the next step in evaluating undiagnosed exudative pleural effusion. It can identify pleural thickening, nodules, lung parenchymal abnormalities, and mediastinal pathology to guide further testing. Clinical pearl: "Pleural effusion workup" — exudate = CT chest. If CT suggests malignancy, next is image-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy. If CT suggests TB, pleural fluid ADA and biopsy for culture.
Repeat thoracentesis has low yield after the first non-diagnostic tap. The fluid characteristics are known (exudate). The next step is imaging and/or pleural biopsy, not another tap.
Bronchoscopy is appropriate if there is a parenchymal lesion or endobronchial abnormality on CT. Without a known lung lesion, the sensitivity of bronchoscopy for pleural disease alone is low.

Empiric TB therapy without microbiologic confirmation is inappropriate. Pleural TB is pauci-bacillary; confirmation requires pleural fluid ADA (>40 U/L), biopsy with granulomas, or pleural fluid culture/genexpert.

rationale: CT chest is the next step in evaluating undiagnosed exudative pleural effusion. It can identify pleural thickening, nodules, lung parenchymal abnormalities, and mediastinal pathology to guide further testing.

question: A 62-year-old with recent COVID-19 pneumonia presents with persistent dyspnea and cough. O2 sat 91% on room air. CXR shows bilateral interstitial opacities. What is the most appropriate long-term management?

options.text: Pulmonary rehabilitation, symptomatic management, follow-up PFTs in 3 months
options.rationale: Post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis/ILD is managed with supportive care (rehabilitation, oxygen if needed) and close follow-up. Most patients improve over 3-12 months. Clinical pearl: "Post-COVID ILD" — ~10-20% develop persistent fibrotic changes. Risk factors: severe COVID, older age, male, pre-existing lung disease. Antifibrotics (nintedanib) are reserved for progressive disease.
Steroids are not recommended for post-COVID fibrotic changes unless there is evidence of organizing pneumonia component or autoimmune disease. Empirical high-dose steroids may worsen outcomes.

rationale: Post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis/ILD is managed with supportive care (rehabilitation, oxygen if needed) and close follow-up. Most patients improve over 3-12 months.

question: A 70-year-old on amiodarone for AF presents with progressive dyspnea, cough, and weight loss. HRCT shows bilateral upper lobe-predominant ground-glass opacities and fibrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary toxicity (5-15% incidence) manifesting as interstitial pneumonitis, organizing pneumonia, or pulmonary fibrosis. It is dose-related (>400 mg/day) but can occur at lower doses. Clinical pearl: "Amiodarone toxicity" — monitor with annual CXR/PFTs. Earliest sign is reduced DLCO. Treatment: stop amiodarone, consider steroids. Mortality is ~10% even with treatment.
IPF has basilar, peripheral predominance (UIP pattern), not upper lobe predominance. The temporal relationship with amiodarone initiation strongly suggests drug toxicity.
HP presents with exposure history (mold, birds), centrilobular nodules, and mosaic attenuation. The upper lobe predominance overlaps but the drug history is the strongest clue.
CTD-ILD (RA, scleroderma) presents with basilar fibrosis and NSIP pattern. While possible, the strong temporal relationship with amiodarone and the upper lobe predominance favor drug toxicity.

rationale: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary toxicity (5-15% incidence) manifesting as interstitial pneumonitis, organizing pneumonia, or pulmonary fibrosis. It is dose-related (>400 mg/day) but can occur at lower doses.

Silicosis causes eggshell calcification of hilar nodes and upper lobe nodular opacities. Erythema nodosum is not a feature of silicosis, and there is no occupational exposure history.

rationale: BHL with erythema nodosum (Löfgren syndrome) is pathognomonic for sarcoidosis. Reduced DLCO indicates pulmonary involvement even with normal lung volumes.

question: A 52-year-old on amiodarone for AF presents with progressive dyspnea, cough, and weight loss. HRCT shows bilateral upper lobe-predominant ground-glass opacities and fibrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

question: A 35-year-old with PE (segmental). sPESI 35 (no risk factors). BP 35/35, O35 35%. No RV strain on echo. What is the most appropriate management setting?

question: A 48-year-old with asthma using SABA 48-48x/week, nocturnal symptoms 48x/week, FEV48 48%. What is the appropriate step-up therapy?

question: A 52-year-old presents with dyspnea and cough. CXR shows a 52 cm solitary pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe. The patient is a 52-pack-year smoker. What is the most appropriate next step?

question: A 30-year-old presents with 3 months of bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from rectum to sigmoid with friable mucosa and crypt abscesses. What is the next step?

question: A 35-year-old presents with RUQ pain, fever 39.5°C, jaundice. Murphy sign positive. US shows gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid. What is the definitive management?

options.text: IV antibiotics + urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours
options.rationale: Acute cholecystitis with fever requires antibiotics and early cholecystectomy (Tokyo Guidelines 2018: Grade I/II). Early surgery (<72 hours) reduces morbidity and hospital stay compared to delayed surgery. Clinical pearl: "Tokyo guidelines" — Grade I (mild): early cholecystectomy. Grade II (moderate): early cholecystectomy if experienced. Grade III (severe): ICU + drainage + delayed cholecystectomy.
ERCP is for choledocholithiasis (CBD stones). This patient has ACUTE CHOLECYSTITIS (gallbladder inflammation), not cholangitis. ERCP does not help gallbladder inflammation.
Delayed cholecystectomy after initial antibiotic therapy increases the risk of recurrent acute cholecystitis, biliary complications (perforation, abscess), and longer total hospital stay.
Cholecystostomy is reserved for Tokyo Grade III (severe) cholecystitis or patients who are too high-risk for surgery. This patient has Grade I/II and should undergo cholecystectomy.

rationale: Acute cholecystitis with fever requires antibiotics and early cholecystectomy (Tokyo Guidelines 2018: Grade I/II). Early surgery (<72 hours) reduces morbidity and hospital stay compared to delayed surgery.

question: A 60-year-old with cirrhosis presents with abdominal distension. Tense ascites, shifting dullness. What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Sodium restriction (2g/day) + spironolactone 100 mg daily + furosemide 40 mg daily
options.rationale: First-line management of cirrhotic ascites is sodium restriction (88 mmol/day) and combination diuretic therapy (spironolactone + furosemide). Spironolactone antagonizes secondary hyperaldosteronism. Clinical pearl: "Ascites management pyramid" — dietary Na restriction + diuretics → large-volume paracentesis → TIPS → liver transplant. LVP is reserved for TENSE ascites causing respiratory compromise or refractory ascites not responding to diuretics. First-line is always medical management with salt restriction and diuretics.
TIPS is for REFRACTORY ascites not responding to medical therapy or recurrent symptomatic ascites requiring frequent paracentesis. It can worsen hepatic encephalopathy.
Albumin is indicated for SBP prophylaxis in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh B/C with ascites) and for prevention of post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction after large-volume (>5L) paracentesis.

rationale: First-line management of cirrhotic ascites is sodium restriction (88 mmol/day) and combination diuretic therapy (spironolactone + furosemide). Spironolactone antagonizes secondary hyperaldosteronism.

question: A 50-year-old presents with hematemesis. EGD shows esophageal varices (large, red wale signs). What is the most appropriate immediate endoscopic intervention?

options.rationale: EVBL is the standard of care for acute variceal hemorrhage and secondary prophylaxis. Band ligation achieves hemostasis in 90% of cases. question: A 25-year-old female with episodic abdominal pain, diarrhea alternating with constipation, and bloating. Normal colonoscopy. Symptoms >6 months. LFTs, ESR, CRP normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Absence of alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, family history of IBD/CRC) supports the diagnosis. Clinical pearl: "Rome IV" — diagnosis of exclusion once alarm features are absent. Trial of low FODMAP diet and tricyclic antidepressants for visceral pain.

Celiac disease presents with diarrhea, weight loss, and malabsorption (steatorrhea, vitamin deficiencies). Serology (tTG IgA) and duodenal biopsy show characteristic changes. Normal colonoscopy does not rule out celiac.

rationale: Rome IV criteria for IBS: recurrent abdominal pain (≥1 day/week in last 3 months) associated with defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool form. Absence of alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, family history of IBD/CRC) supports the diagnosis.

question: A 40-year-old alcoholic presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting. Lipase 2500 U/L. Pancreatic calcifications on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: CT shows pancreatic calcifications (chronic pancreatitis) with acute inflammation (lipase >3x normal, pain). This represents acute exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis. Clinical pearl: "Pancreatitis causes" — get the "I GET SMASHED" mnemonic: Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion stings, Hyperlipidemia, Hypercalcemia, ERCP, Drugs.
Hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis occurs with TG >1000 mg/dL. No lipid levels are mentioned, and the CT shows pancreatic calcifications indicating chronic changes from alcohol.

Pancreatic pseudocyst forms 4-6 weeks after acute pancreatitis and presents with persistent pain, early satiety, or a palpable mass. The acute pain + lipase elevation is consistent with acute pancreatitis exacerbation.
Pancreatic cancer presents with painless jaundice, weight loss, and a pancreatic mass. Lipase is minimally elevated. Calcifications indicate chronic pancreatitis, not malignancy.

rationale: CT shows pancreatic calcifications (chronic pancreatitis) with acute inflammation (lipase >3x normal, pain). This represents acute exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis.

question: A 65-year-old on warfarin for AF presents with melena and hematemesis. BP 90/60, HR 110. Hb 7.5. INR 4.5. What is the appropriate management?

options.text: IV fluids, blood transfusion, vitamin K 10 mg IV, 4-factor PCC 25 U/kg, urgent EGD
options.rationale: Life-threatening GI bleed on warfarin with INR >4 requires REVERSAL (vitamin K + PCC/FFP) + resuscitation + urgent endoscopy. PCC reverses INR in 15 min vs FFP (hours) with less volume. Clinical pearl: "Warfarin reversal" — PCC + vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding. Vitamin K alone takes 6-24 hours. FFP for PCC unavailable. DOAC reversal with andexanet alfa (Xa inhibitors) or idarucizumab (dabigatran).

Active GI bleeding with hemodynamic instability requires immediate reversal, not just holding warfarin. Warfarin has a half-life of 36-48 hours; holding alone will not reverse anticoagulation fast enough.
FFP provides some reversal but requires ABO compatibility, takes time to thaw, and large volumes can cause volume overload. PCC is preferred for more complete and rapid reversal.
DDAVP releases von Willebrand factor and is used for uremic bleeding or vWD, not warfarin reversal. It has no effect on vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency.

rationale: Life-threatening GI bleed on warfarin with INR >4 requires REVERSAL (vitamin K + PCC/FFP) + resuscitation + urgent endoscopy. PCC reverses INR in 15 min vs FFP (hours) with less volume.

question: A 30-year-old male with Crohn's disease presents with a 4-day history of RLQ pain, fever, and a palpable mass. CT shows a phlegmonous mass surrounding a thickened terminal ileum. What is the most appropriate management?

Surgery is reserved for failure, frank perforation, or drainable abscess. Clinical pearl: "Crohn's complications" — phlegmon: medical Rx.
