Radiation is third-line due to delayed effect (5-10 years), hypopituitarism risk (50-80% at 10 years), and risk of secondary brain tumors. Used for residual disease after surgery and failed medical therapy.

rationale: First-line therapy for acromegaly is surgical resection (transsphenoidal). Cure rates are 80-90% for microadenomas and 50-60% for macroadenomas without cavernous sinus invasion.

question: A 72-year-old female presents with oligomenorrhea, galactorrhea, and headaches. Prolactin 72 ng/mL. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: MRI pituitary + start cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly
options.rationale: Hyperprolactinemia (prolactin >200 ng/mL is almost always from a prolactinoma) requires pituitary MRI to evaluate for macroadenoma (>1 cm). Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are first-line therapy, normalizing prolactin in 85% and shrinking tumor in 80%. Clinical pearl: "Prolactinoma management" — cabergoline > bromocriptine (better tolerated, more effective). Stop if pregnancy is desired. If macroprolactinoma, continue through pregnancy. Surgery if resistant.

options.text: Start bromocriptine 2.5 mg BID without imaging
options.rationale: Imaging is necessary to assess tumor size and exclude a non-functioning pituitary mass causing stalk effect (moderate prolactin elevation <200). Dopamine agonist therapy can proceed after imaging.
Surgery is second-line for prolactinomas, reserved for dopamine agonist resistance, intolerance, or apoplexy. Medical therapy is first-line.
OCPs regulate menses but do not treat the underlying prolactinoma. The patient has a tumor causing galactorrhea and headache that requires specific therapy (dopamine agonist), not symptom masking.

rationale: Hyperprolactinemia (prolactin >200 ng/mL is almost always from a prolactinoma) requires pituitary MRI to evaluate for macroadenoma (>1 cm). Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are first-line therapy, normalizing prolactin in 85% and shrinking tumor in 80%.

question: A 45-year-old with obesity (BMI 45), T45DM, OSA, and HTN. HbA45c 45.45% on metformin + semaglutide 45 mg weekly. What is the most appropriate weight loss intervention?

options.text: Increase semaglutide to 2.4 mg weekly (Wegovy dose) or switch to tirzepatide
options.rationale: Semaglutide 2.4 mg (Wegovy) is FDA-approved for weight management and provides average 15% weight loss. Tirzepatide (Zepbound) provides up to 22% weight loss at 15 mg. Per ADA 2024, GLP-1 RA with proven weight efficacy is preferred in patients with obesity. Clinical pearl: "Anti-obesity medications" — GLP-1 RA (semaglutide 2.4mg, liraglutide 3.0mg), dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide 15mg), phentermine/topiramate, bupropion/naltrexone. Bariatric surgery for BMI >40 or >35 with comorbidities.

Bariatric surgery is indicated for BMI >40 or >35 with obesity-related comorbidities after failed medical management. Medical therapy (increased-dose semaglutide or tirzepatide) should be optimized first.
Phentermine is FDA-approved for short-term use (12 weeks) only. It has limited efficacy for long-term weight management and provides less weight loss than GLP-1 RA.

Intragastric balloon is a third-line option for BMI 30-40. It provides modest weight loss (10-15%) with side effects (nausea, vomiting, balloon deflation risk). Pharmacotherapy should be optimized first.

rationale: Semaglutide 2.4 mg (Wegovy) is FDA-approved for weight management and provides average 15% weight loss. Tirzepatide (Zepbound) provides up to 22% weight loss at 15 mg.

question: A 50-year-old with DM and CKD eGFR 50 has HbA50c of 50.50% on metformin + gliclazide. What should be done?

options.text: Reduce gliclazide dose, consider de-intensification (avoid hypoglycemia)
options.rationale: In older adults with CKD and DM, less stringent glycemic targets (HbA1c 7-8%) are recommended to avoid hypoglycemia. A HbA1c of 6.2% indicates overtreatment. Clinical pearl: "De-intensification in elderly" — ADA 2024: for older adults with multiple comorbidities, HbA1c <8% is acceptable. De-intensify sulfonylureas or insulin to avoid hypoglycemia which causes falls, cognitive impairment, and CV events.

While 6.2% seems good, in elderly CKD patients, this level of control likely causes significant hypoglycemia (especially with sulfonylurea). The risks of hypoglycemia (falls, MCI, death) outweigh the benefits of tight control.

options.text: Add insulin glargine for tighter control
options.rationale: Adding insulin would worsen hypoglycemia risk. The patient is already over-controlled. De-intensification, not intensification, is needed.

options.text: Switch to dapagliflozin and stop gliclazide
options.rationale: While SGLT2i are beneficial in CKD, they are less effective at HbA1c reduction (~0.5%). The main issue here is overtreatment, not therapy choice. De-intensification remains the priority.

rationale: In older adults with CKD and DM, less stringent glycemic targets (HbA1c 7-8%) are recommended to avoid hypoglycemia. A HbA1c of 6.2% indicates overtreatment.

question: A 42-year-old male with thyroid nodule. US shows a 42.42 cm solid nodule with microcalcifications. TIRADS 42. TSH 42.42. FNA: suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma (Bethesda V). What is the management?

options.text: Total thyroidectomy vs lobectomy (papillary thyroid carcinoma)
options.rationale: Bethesda V (suspicious for malignancy) has 60-75% PPV for cancer. ATA guidelines recommend total thyroidectomy for nodules >4 cm, bilateral nodules, extrathyroidal extension, or LN metastasis. Lobectomy is sufficient for unifocal, <4 cm, intrathyroidal PTC. Clinical pearl: "Thyroid nodule management" — TIRADS 5: FNA indicated. Bethesda V/VI: surgery. Bethesda III/IV: repeat FNA or molecular testing. Post-op: RAI if high-risk features. TSH suppression based on recurrence risk.
CT is not needed for surgical planning unless there is concern for extensive lymph node metastasis or substernal extension. US provides adequate information for most thyroid surgeries.
Bethesda V warrants surgery, not surveillance. The risk of malignancy is >60%. Delaying diagnosis could allow progression to more advanced disease.
RAI is adjuvant therapy AFTER surgery for high-risk PTC (residual disease, LN mets, aggressive variants). It is not primary therapy. Surgery is required for tissue diagnosis and removal.

rationale: Bethesda V (suspicious for malignancy) has 60-75% PPV for cancer. ATA guidelines recommend total thyroidectomy for nodules >4 cm, bilateral nodules, extrathyroidal extension, or LN metastasis.

question: A 38-year-old female with secondary amenorrhea, hyponatremia (Na 38). She is on no medications. Cortisol 38 (low), ACTH 38 (inappropriately normal). What is the most likely cause?

options.rationale: Secondary amenorrhea + hyponatremia + low cortisol with inappropriately NORMAL ACTH = secondary adrenal insufficiency. Sheehan syndrome (postpartum hemorrhage leading to pituitary infarction) is a classic cause. Clinical pearl: "Sheehan syndrome" — occurs 0-14 days after delivery. Presents with failure to lactate, amenorrhea, fatigue, hyponatremia. MRI shows empty sella. Treatment: hormone replacement (glucocorticoid first, then levothyroxine, then estrogen).
Primary AI (Addison) would show HIGH ACTH, not inappropriately normal. The low-normal ACTH localizes the problem to the pituitary or hypothalamus.

Hyponatremia in adrenal insufficiency is from cortisol deficiency (impairs free water excretion). It is NOT SIADH (which requires normal adrenal function). Treating with steroids corrects the hyponatremia.
Autoimmune hypophysitis can cause secondary adrenal insufficiency but is less common than Sheehan syndrome. It can present with headache, visual field defects, and pituitary enlargement on MRI.

rationale: Secondary amenorrhea + hyponatremia + low cortisol with inappropriately NORMAL ACTH = secondary adrenal insufficiency. Sheehan syndrome (postpartum hemorrhage leading to pituitary infarction) is a classic cause.

question: A 55-year-old with T55DM on metformin 55g/day and lifestyle. HbA55c 55.55%. BMI 55. What is the next appropriate agent?

options.text: Add GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide 0.5 mg SC weekly)
options.rationale: Per ADA 2024 guidelines, GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i are preferred add-on agents after metformin, especially in patients with obesity or ASCVD/HF/CKD. Semaglutide has demonstrated HbA1c reduction of 1.5-1.8% AND significant weight loss (SUSTAIN, STEP trials). Clinical pearl: "Diabetes drug selection" — ASCVD/HF/CKD: GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i. Obesity: GLP-1 RA. Cost: sulfonylurea or TZD. No ASCVD: metformin + lifestyle.
Sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia. In an obese patient with HbA1c 8.5%, a GLP-1 RA provides better glycemic control AND weight loss without hypoglycemia risk.
TZDs cause weight gain, fluid retention (risk of HF decompensation), and increased fracture risk. They are less preferred in obesity. GLP-1 RA has superior weight and glucose outcomes.
DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral and have modest HbA1c reduction (~0.5-0.7%). They are less effective than GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i for weight loss and do not have cardiovascular benefits.

rationale: Per ADA 2024 guidelines, GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i are preferred add-on agents after metformin, especially in patients with obesity or ASCVD/HF/CKD. Semaglutide has demonstrated HbA1c reduction of 1.5-1.8% AND significant weight loss (SUSTAIN, STEP trials).

question: A 58-year-old female presents with weight loss, palpitations, tremor. TSH <58.58, free T58 58.58, TPO antibodies positive. Thyroid exam: diffuse goiter with bruit. What is the best initial therapy?

options.rationale: Graves disease in a non-pregnant patient is treated with methimazole (thionamide) plus beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms. Methimazole blocks thyroid peroxidase, reducing hormone synthesis. Clinical pearl: "Graves management" — Treat with methimazole 12-18 months. Check TSH/T4 q4-6 weeks initially. Titrate to lowest effective dose. Relapse rate after 12-18 months: 40-60%. Definitive therapy (RAI or surgery) for relapse.
RAI is appropriate for definitive therapy but not initial therapy in young patients. RAI is avoided in active thyroid eye disease (can worsen TED). Methimazole is typically trialed first.
Beta-blockers control symptoms but do NOT lower thyroid hormone levels. Without antithyroid therapy, the patient remains at high risk for complications (AFib, thyroid storm, osteoporosis).
Steroids are reserved for thyroid storm (in addition to thionamides), severe orbitopathy, or subacute (viral) thyroiditis. They are not first-line for uncomplicated Graves disease.

rationale: Graves disease in a non-pregnant patient is treated with methimazole (thionamide) plus beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms. Methimazole blocks thyroid peroxidase, reducing hormone synthesis.

question: A 60-year-old on metformin + empagliflozin. HbA60c 60.60%. eGFR 60 mL/min. What is the appropriate adjustment?

options.text: Stop metformin (eGFR <30), continue empagliflozin, add insulin
options.rationale: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR <30 (lactic acidosis risk). Empagliflozin can be continued down to eGFR 20. Adding insulin is appropriate for glycemic control in CKD. Clinical pearl: "Metformin and CKD" — eGFR 30-45: max 1000mg/day. eGFR <30: contraindicated. SGLT2i: continue to eGFR 20. GLP-1 RA: no renal adjustment except liraglutide (caution in ESRD). Insulin: preferred in advanced CKD.

options.text: Reduce metformin to 500mg BID, continue empagliflozin
options.rationale: Metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30 regardless of dose. The risk of lactic acidosis outweighs any glycemic benefit. Metformin should be discontinued.

Sulfonylureas (especially long-acting) carry significant hypoglycemia risk in CKD due to reduced clearance. If an oral agent is needed, a DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin, linagliptin) adjusted for renal function or a short-acting secretagogue (repaglinide) is safer.

While sitagliptin can be used in CKD (dose-adjusted to 25 mg for eGFR <30), glycemia is high (HbA1c 9.2%). DPP-4 inhibitors are modestly effective (~0.5% reduction). Insulin is more appropriate for this level of hyperglycemia.

rationale: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR <30 (lactic acidosis risk). Empagliflozin can be continued down to eGFR 20.

question: A 62-year-old female presents with recurrent nephrolithiasis. Calcium 62.62, PTH 62 (elevated), 62-OH D 62, phosphate 62.62. What is the most appropriate confirmatory test?

options.text: DEXA scan + 24-hour urine calcium + sestamibi scan
options.rationale: Primary hyperparathyroidism (high Ca + high PTH) requires (1) DEXA for bone density assessment, (2) 24h urine Ca to rule out familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), (3) sestamibi scan to localize adenoma. Clinical pearl: "PHPT workup" — FHH has low 24h urine Ca (<100 mg), high Ca, and normal-to-high PTH. Parathyroidectomy is indicated for classic PHPT, not FHH.
Pituitary causes of hypercalcemia are extremely rare (MEN1-related hyperparathyroidism is the most common MEN1 manifestation). The pituitary is not the primary driver in most cases.
Sarcoidosis causes hypercalcemia via extrarenal 1-alpha hydroxylase but would show LOW PTH (suppressed by high Ca). Elevated PTH rules out granulomatous disease.

options.text: Repeat calcium, PTH, and vitamin D in 3 months
options.rationale: The patient already has confirmed hypercalcemia (Ca 11.0) with elevated PTH and a complication (nephrolithiasis). Surgical intervention is indicated — no need to delay with repeat labs.

rationale: Primary hyperparathyroidism (high Ca + high PTH) requires (1) DEXA for bone density assessment, (2) 24h urine Ca to rule out familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), (3) sestamibi scan to localize adenoma. Clinical pearl: "PHPT workup" — FHH has low 24h urine Ca (<100 mg), high Ca, and normal-to-high PTH.

question: A 65-year-old with incidentally found 65.65 cm adrenal mass (incidentaloma). BP 65/65, K+ 65.65. No symptoms. What is the most appropriate evaluation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test + plasma metanephrines + aldosterone/renin ratio
options.rationale: Adrenal incidentaloma evaluation includes: (1) hormonal testing for Cushing (1mg DST), pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines), and hyperaldosteronism (if HTN/hypokalemia), (2) CT with contrast (Hounsfield units <10 = benign adenoma, >10 = indeterminate). Clinical pearl: "Incidentaloma algorithm" — all need hormonal workup. Lesions >4 cm: consider resection. Lesions <4 cm: if benign by CT and non-functional, follow with repeat imaging at 6-12 months.

Biopsy of adrenal masses is rarely needed and carries risks (bleeding, pneumothorax, pheochromocytoma crisis if not pretreated). It is reserved for suspected metastasis when imaging and labs are inconclusive.

Surgery is indicated for functional tumors (any size), or non-functional tumors >4 cm, or tumors with suspicious imaging features (irregular margins, rapid growth). A 1.5 cm non-functional, benign-appearing adenoma can be followed.

options.text: MRI abdomen with and without contrast
options.rationale: CT is preferred for initial adrenal mass characterization (HU measurement is best on CT). MRI (chemical shift) can characterize lipid-rich vs lipid-poor adenomas but is not first-line.

rationale: Adrenal incidentaloma evaluation includes: (1) hormonal testing for Cushing (1mg DST), pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines), and hyperaldosteronism (if HTN/hypokalemia), (2) CT with contrast (Hounsfield units <10 = benign adenoma, >10 = indeterminate). Clinical pearl: "Incidentaloma algorithm" — all need hormonal workup.

question: A 68-year-old with T68DM on metformin + dapagliflozin + semaglutide. HbA68c 68.68%. What is the next step?

options.text: Add insulin (basal insulin glargine 10 units daily)
options.rationale: When HbA1c is >9% on 3 oral/injectable agents, insulin therapy is indicated. Per ADA 2024 guidelines, basal insulin (NPH or glargine) is the preferred first insulin. Start at 10U or 0.1-0.2 U/kg. Clinical pearl: "Advancing to insulin" — start basal insulin 10U or 0.1-0.2 U/kg. Titrate 2U q3d to target fasting BG 80-130. If HbA1c remains above target, add prandial insulin before largest meal.
Adding a fourth agent (TZD) without insulin is unlikely to be effective at HbA1c 9.5%. Also, TZDs cause weight gain and fluid retention, which counteracts the benefits of SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA.
Sulfonylureas are less effective when HbA1c is >9% and carry hypoglycemia risk. At this level of hyperglycemia, the patient likely has significant beta-cell dysfunction requiring insulin.

options.text: Switch from semaglutide to tirzepatide 5 mg weekly
options.rationale: While tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1 RA) is more potent than semaglutide, switching from one injectable to another is unlikely to achieve the needed glycemic reduction. Insulin is indicated.

rationale: When HbA1c is >9% on 3 oral/injectable agents, insulin therapy is indicated. Per ADA 2024 guidelines, basal insulin (NPH or glargine) is the preferred first insulin.

question: A 70-year-old presents with fatigue, pallor. Hb 7.0, MCV 110, B12 150 (low), folate normal, reticulocyte count 0.5%. Peripheral smear: macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intrinsic factor antibodies + anti-parietal cell antibodies + start B12 injections
options.rationale: B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and low reticulocyte count (indicating bone marrow suppression) requires prompt B12 replacement AND investigation for pernicious anemia (IF antibodies, anti-parietal cell antibodies). Clinical pearl: "Pernicious anemia" — autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption. Treat with IM B12 1000mcg weekly x4 weeks then monthly. Monitor for gastric carcinoid (increased risk in autoimmune gastritis).
Folic acid alone in B12 deficiency can correct the anemia but allow neurologic complications (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) to progress. Folate should only be given if B12 is normal.
Bone marrow biopsy is not needed if the diagnosis is clear (low B12, macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, low retics). It is reserved for unexplained cytopenias or suspected myelodysplasia.
While pernicious anemia is associated with autoimmune gastritis and increased gastric cancer risk, the immediate priority is B12 replacement. Endoscopy can be arranged electively, not emergently.

rationale: B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and low reticulocyte count (indicating bone marrow suppression) requires prompt B12 replacement AND investigation for pernicious anemia (IF antibodies, anti-parietal cell antibodies). Clinical pearl: "Pernicious anemia" — autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption.

question: A 45-year-old female presents with petechiae, epistaxis. Platelets 15,000. Hb 13, WBC normal. Splenomegaly absent. What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: High-dose dexamethasone 40 mg daily x4 days (pulse steroids)
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) with platelets <30,000 requires treatment to prevent bleeding. First-line therapy is corticosteroids: pulse dexamethasone (40 mg x4 days) or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 3-4 weeks. Clinical pearl: "ITP management" — first-line: steroids + IVIG if needed for rapid rise. Second-line: TPO-RA (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy. TPO-RA are preferred over splenectomy now.
IVIG produces rapid platelet rise (within 24-48h) but is reserved for severe bleeding or as a bridge to steroids. Steroids are first-line as they are cheaper and provide sustained response.
Rituximab is second-line therapy in ITP. It takes 2-4 weeks to work and is reserved for steroid-refractory or relapsed disease.
Platelet transfusions in ITP are ineffective (antibodies destroy transfused platelets rapidly). They are reserved for life-threatening bleeding (ICH, GI bleeding) in combination with IVIG.

rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) with platelets <30,000 requires treatment to prevent bleeding. First-line therapy is corticosteroids: pulse dexamethasone (40 mg x4 days) or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 3-4 weeks.

question: A 60-year-old with fatigue, bone pain. Hb 9.5, Cr 2.0, Ca 11.0. SPEP: M-spike 3.5 g/dL. Serum free light chain ratio elevated. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy + skeletal survey + start treatment if biopsy confirms myeloma
options.rationale: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by CRAB criteria (Calcium elevation, Renal impairment, Anemia, Bone lesions) plus ≥10% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow biopsy. Skeletal survey (not bone scan) detects lytic lesions. Clinical pearl: "Multiple myeloma" — MGUS (<10% plasma cells, no CRAB) vs Smoldering (>10% plasma cells, no CRAB) vs Active (≥10% plasma cells + CRAB/SLiM criteria). Treatment: non-transplant candidates: VRd (bortezomib + lenalidomide + dexamethasone).
PET-CT can detect extramedullary disease and is increasingly used but is not the first step. Bone marrow biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and assess plasma cell percentage is critical.
Treatment should not start without tissue diagnosis (bone marrow biopsy confirms ≥10% plasma cells). MGUS and smoldering myeloma do not require immediate treatment.

options.text: Refer for autologous stem cell transplant
options.rationale: ASCT is consolidation therapy after induction chemotherapy, not first-line therapy. Induction with VRd (or other triplet) is given first, then stem cell harvest, then ASCT.

rationale: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by CRAB criteria (Calcium elevation, Renal impairment, Anemia, Bone lesions) plus ≥10% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow biopsy. Skeletal survey (not bone scan) detects lytic lesions.

question: A 25-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with severe chest pain, fever, hypoxia (O2 sat 88%), and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV fluids, antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin), O2, incentive spirometry, exchange transfusion if worsening
options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a leading cause of death in SCD. Treatment includes (1) O2 for hypoxia, (2) antibiotics (atypical + typical coverage), (3) bronchodilators, (4) incentive spirometry (reduces atelectasis), (5) simple transfusion for Hb <9, (6) exchange transfusion for severe/worsening ACS. Clinical pearl: "ACS triggers" — infection, fat embolism, atelectasis, pulmonary infarction. Prevention: hydroxyurea reduces ACS episodes by 50%.
Hydroxyurea is prevention (reduces crisis frequency), not acute treatment. ACS requires emergent interventions: O2, antibiotics, transfusion. Hydroxyurea is started when stable.
Steroids are not standard for ACS and may increase vaso-occlusive complications. Some regimens use short-course steroids for severe inflammation, but antibiotics and transfusion are the priority.
Inhaled NO is not proven effective for ACS (NO trial in SCD was negative). Supportive care with O2, antibiotics, and transfusion as needed remains the standard.

rationale: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a leading cause of death in SCD. Treatment includes (1) O2 for hypoxia, (2) antibiotics (atypical + typical coverage), (3) bronchodilators, (4) incentive spirometry (reduces atelectasis), (5) simple transfusion for Hb <9, (6) exchange transfusion for severe/worsening ACS.

question: A 35-year-old female presents with recurrent DVT (2 episodes). Workup: prolonged aPTT. Mixing study: does NOT correct. Anti-cardiolipin antibodies positive. What is the appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Lifelong warfarin with target INR 2-3 (or 3-4 for recurrent thrombosis)
options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) with recurrent thrombosis requires indefinite anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3 for first DVT, 3-4 for recurrent). DOACs are contraindicated in APS (especially triple-positive) due to increased thrombosis risk (TRAPS trial showed rivaroxaban INCREASED events). Clinical pearl: "APS triple-positive" — LA + aCL + aβ2GPI = highest risk. Warfarin is the ONLY anticoagulant proven effective. DOACs are contraindicated.
DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are CONTRAINDICATED in APS due to higher rates of recurrent thrombosis (TRAPS, RAPS trials). Warfarin is the standard of care.

options.text: LMWH bridge to warfarin for 3 months
options.rationale: Three months of anticoagulation is inadequate for unprovoked DVT, especially in APS with recurrent thrombosis. Lifelong anticoagulation is indicated.
Aspirin is inadequate for venous thromboembolism. APS requires full anticoagulation with warfarin. Aspirin may be used for primary thrombosis prevention in asymptomatic APS carriers.

rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) with recurrent thrombosis requires indefinite anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3 for first DVT, 3-4 for recurrent). DOACs are contraindicated in APS (especially triple-positive) due to increased thrombosis risk (TRAPS trial showed rivaroxaban INCREASED events).

question: A 80-year-old male with metastatic prostate cancer presents with fatigue. Hb 8.0, MCV 78. Ferritin 30, iron 30, TIBC 450, TSAT 7%. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss
options.rationale: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin, low iron, low TSAT, and high TIBC = iron deficiency. In an elderly male, GI blood loss (malignancy, angiodysplasia, ulcer) is the likely source. Clinical pearl: "Iron deficiency workup" — in men and postmenopausal women, always evaluate for GI bleeding (EGD + colonoscopy). Low ferritin (<30) is the most specific marker. In inflammation, ferritin can be falsely normal.
ACD would show normal-to-high ferritin, low iron, low TIBC, and normal TSAT (~20%). High TIBC is specific to iron deficiency. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant and is elevated in ACD.
MDS would present with macrocytic anemia (high MCV), not microcytic. Additionally, blast counts and cytopenias would be evident on peripheral smear and bone marrow.

Thalassemia trait causes microcytic anemia but with normal or ELEVATED RBC count, normal iron studies, and Hb electrophoresis showing elevated HbA2. This patient has clear iron deficiency (low ferritin, high TIBC).

rationale: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin, low iron, low TSAT, and high TIBC = iron deficiency. In an elderly male, GI blood loss (malignancy, angiodysplasia, ulcer) is the likely source.

question: A 65-year-old with myelofibrosis presents with massive splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, and transfusion-dependent anemia. What is the most appropriate therapy?

options.rationale: Ruxolitinib is first-line therapy for intermediate-2 or high-risk myelofibrosis. It reduces splenomegaly (~50% reduction at 6 months), improves constitutional symptoms, and prolongs survival (COMFORT-I/II trials). Clinical pearl: "MPN management" — Myelofibrosis: ruxolitinib. Essential thrombocythemia: hydroxyurea or anagrelide. Polycythemia vera: phlebotomy + low-dose aspirin. All MPNs have increased thrombosis and leukemic transformation risk.

Splenectomy carries significant risks in myelofibrosis (bleeding, infection, thrombotic complications, accelerated hepatomegaly). It is reserved for refractory symptomatic splenomegaly not responding to JAK2 inhibitors.
Hydroxyurea is used for ET and PV but is not effective for myelofibrosis-associated splenomegaly. Ruxolitinib has specifically demonstrated disease-modifying effects in MF.
Interferon is used for PV and ET (especially in younger patients) but has limited efficacy in MF and significant side effects (flu-like symptoms, depression, fatigue).

rationale: Ruxolitinib is first-line therapy for intermediate-2 or high-risk myelofibrosis. It reduces splenomegaly (~50% reduction at 6 months), improves constitutional symptoms, and prolongs survival (COMFORT-I/II trials).

question: A 55-year-old presents with axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Biopsy: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, PAX5+). What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, PAX5 weak+) in the appropriate background (reactive lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells) = classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL). Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype. Clinical pearl: "Hodgkin lymphoma" — treatment depends on stage: early-stage (I-II): ABVD x2-4 cycles + involved-field RT. Advanced (III-IV): ABVD x6. PET-CT for interim response assessment guides escalation/de-escalation. Cure rate: 80-90%.
DLBCL cells are CD20+, CD45+, not Reed-Sternberg cells. They lack CD15 and CD30 expression. The morphology is centroblastic or immunoblastic.
ALCL also expresses CD30 but is a T-cell lymphoma (CD3+, CD45RO+). It shows hallmark cells with horseshoe nuclei, NOT Reed-Sternberg cells with owl-eye nucleoli.
NLPHL has LP cells (popcorn cells), not classical RS cells. LP cells are CD20+, CD15-, CD30-, a different immunophenotype requiring different management.

rationale: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, PAX5 weak+) in the appropriate background (reactive lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells) = classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL). Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype.

question: A 50-year-old presents with fatigue, pallor. Hb 50.50, MCV 50, B50 50 (low), folate normal, reticulocyte count 50.50%. Peripheral smear: macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intrinsic factor antibodies + anti-parietal cell antibodies + start B12 injections
options.rationale: B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and low reticulocyte count (indicating bone marrow suppression) requires prompt B12 replacement AND investigation for pernicious anemia (IF antibodies, anti-parietal cell antibodies). Clinical pearl: "Pernicious anemia" — autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption. Treat with IM B12 1000mcg weekly x4 weeks then monthly. Monitor for gastric carcinoid (increased risk in autoimmune gastritis).
Folic acid alone in B12 deficiency can correct the anemia but allow neurologic complications (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) to progress. Folate should only be given if B12 is normal.
Bone marrow biopsy is not needed if the diagnosis is clear (low B12, macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, low retics). It is reserved for unexplained cytopenias or suspected myelodysplasia.
While pernicious anemia is associated with autoimmune gastritis and increased gastric cancer risk, the immediate priority is B12 replacement. Endoscopy can be arranged electively, not emergently.

rationale: B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and low reticulocyte count (indicating bone marrow suppression) requires prompt B12 replacement AND investigation for pernicious anemia (IF antibodies, anti-parietal cell antibodies). Clinical pearl: "Pernicious anemia" — autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption.

question: A 42-year-old female presents with petechiae, epistaxis. Platelets 42,42. Hb 42, WBC normal. Splenomegaly absent. What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: High-dose dexamethasone 40 mg daily x4 days (pulse steroids)
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) with platelets <30,000 requires treatment to prevent bleeding. First-line therapy is corticosteroids: pulse dexamethasone (40 mg x4 days) or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 3-4 weeks. Clinical pearl: "ITP management" — first-line: steroids + IVIG if needed for rapid rise. Second-line: TPO-RA (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy. TPO-RA are preferred over splenectomy now.
IVIG produces rapid platelet rise (within 24-48h) but is reserved for severe bleeding or as a bridge to steroids. Steroids are first-line as they are cheaper and provide sustained response.
Rituximab is second-line therapy in ITP. It takes 2-4 weeks to work and is reserved for steroid-refractory or relapsed disease.
Platelet transfusions in ITP are ineffective (antibodies destroy transfused platelets rapidly). They are reserved for life-threatening bleeding (ICH, GI bleeding) in combination with IVIG.

rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) with platelets <30,000 requires treatment to prevent bleeding. First-line therapy is corticosteroids: pulse dexamethasone (40 mg x4 days) or prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 3-4 weeks.

question: A 38-year-old with fatigue, bone pain. Hb 38.38, Cr 38.38, Ca 38.38. SPEP: M-spike 38.38 g/dL. Serum free light chain ratio elevated. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy + skeletal survey + start treatment if biopsy confirms myeloma
options.rationale: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by CRAB criteria (Calcium elevation, Renal impairment, Anemia, Bone lesions) plus ≥10% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow biopsy. Skeletal survey (not bone scan) detects lytic lesions. Clinical pearl: "Multiple myeloma" — MGUS (<10% plasma cells, no CRAB) vs Smoldering (>10% plasma cells, no CRAB) vs Active (≥10% plasma cells + CRAB/SLiM criteria). Treatment: non-transplant candidates: VRd (bortezomib + lenalidomide + dexamethasone).
PET-CT can detect extramedullary disease and is increasingly used but is not the first step. Bone marrow biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and assess plasma cell percentage is critical.
Treatment should not start without tissue diagnosis (bone marrow biopsy confirms ≥10% plasma cells). MGUS and smoldering myeloma do not require immediate treatment.

options.text: Refer for autologous stem cell transplant
options.rationale: ASCT is consolidation therapy after induction chemotherapy, not first-line therapy. Induction with VRd (or other triplet) is given first, then stem cell harvest, then ASCT.

rationale: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by CRAB criteria (Calcium elevation, Renal impairment, Anemia, Bone lesions) plus ≥10% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow biopsy. Skeletal survey (not bone scan) detects lytic lesions.

question: A 35-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with severe chest pain, fever, hypoxia (O35 sat 35%), and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV fluids, antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin), O2, incentive spirometry, exchange transfusion if worsening
options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a leading cause of death in SCD. Treatment includes (1) O2 for hypoxia, (2) antibiotics (atypical + typical coverage), (3) bronchodilators, (4) incentive spirometry (reduces atelectasis), (5) simple transfusion for Hb <9, (6) exchange transfusion for severe/worsening ACS. Clinical pearl: "ACS triggers" — infection, fat embolism, atelectasis, pulmonary infarction. Prevention: hydroxyurea reduces ACS episodes by 50%.
Hydroxyurea is prevention (reduces crisis frequency), not acute treatment. ACS requires emergent interventions: O2, antibiotics, transfusion. Hydroxyurea is started when stable.
Steroids are not standard for ACS and may increase vaso-occlusive complications. Some regimens use short-course steroids for severe inflammation, but antibiotics and transfusion are the priority.
Inhaled NO is not proven effective for ACS (NO trial in SCD was negative). Supportive care with O2, antibiotics, and transfusion as needed remains the standard.

rationale: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a leading cause of death in SCD. Treatment includes (1) O2 for hypoxia, (2) antibiotics (atypical + typical coverage), (3) bronchodilators, (4) incentive spirometry (reduces atelectasis), (5) simple transfusion for Hb <9, (6) exchange transfusion for severe/worsening ACS.

question: A 48-year-old male presents with recurrent DVT (48 episodes). Workup: prolonged aPTT. Mixing study: does NOT correct. Anti-cardiolipin antibodies positive. What is the appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Lifelong warfarin with target INR 2-3 (or 3-4 for recurrent thrombosis)
options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) with recurrent thrombosis requires indefinite anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3 for first DVT, 3-4 for recurrent). DOACs are contraindicated in APS (especially triple-positive) due to increased thrombosis risk (TRAPS trial showed rivaroxaban INCREASED events). Clinical pearl: "APS triple-positive" — LA + aCL + aβ2GPI = highest risk. Warfarin is the ONLY anticoagulant proven effective. DOACs are contraindicated.
DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are CONTRAINDICATED in APS due to higher rates of recurrent thrombosis (TRAPS, RAPS trials). Warfarin is the standard of care.

options.text: LMWH bridge to warfarin for 3 months
options.rationale: Three months of anticoagulation is inadequate for unprovoked DVT, especially in APS with recurrent thrombosis. Lifelong anticoagulation is indicated.
Aspirin is inadequate for venous thromboembolism. APS requires full anticoagulation with warfarin. Aspirin may be used for primary thrombosis prevention in asymptomatic APS carriers.

rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) with recurrent thrombosis requires indefinite anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3 for first DVT, 3-4 for recurrent). DOACs are contraindicated in APS (especially triple-positive) due to increased thrombosis risk (TRAPS trial showed rivaroxaban INCREASED events).

question: A 35-year-old with HIV (CD4 150, not on ART) presents with fever, cough, dyspnea. CXR: diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. LDH 500. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: HIV with CD4 <200 + subacute onset of fever/cough/dyspnea + diffuse interstitial infiltrates + elevated LDH = PJP until proven otherwise. Clinical pearl: "PJP in HIV" — diagnosis: induced sputum or BAL with PCR/silver stain. Treatment: TMP-SMX (15-20mg/kg TMP divided q8h) for 21 days. Add prednisone if pO2 <70 or A-a gradient >35 (reduces mortality in moderate-severe PJP). Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX DS daily for CD4 <200.
Bacterial CAP presents with acute onset (hours-days), lobar consolidation on CXR, and purulent sputum. The subacute onset and diffuse interstitial pattern are more consistent with PJP.
TB in HIV presents with upper lobe infiltrates, cavitary lesions, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. CD4 <200 may have atypical presentation but usually not bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates.
CMV pneumonitis occurs when CD4 <50, not 150. It presents with reticular-nodular opacities. While possible, PJP is far more common at CD4 150.

rationale: HIV with CD4 <200 + subacute onset of fever/cough/dyspnea + diffuse interstitial infiltrates + elevated LDH = PJP until proven otherwise. Clinical pearl: "PJP in HIV" — diagnosis: induced sputum or BAL with PCR/silver stain.

question: A 28-year-old with fever, headache, neck stiffness. CSF: WBC 800 (80% lymphocytes), protein 120, glucose 25. What is the most likely cause?

options.rationale: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with low-normal glucose and elevated protein = viral/aseptic meningitis. Enterovirus is the most common cause. HSV and VZV cause more severe disease. Clinical pearl: "Meningitis differentiation" — Bacterial: PMN predominance, very low glucose, high protein. Viral: lymphocytes, normal/low glucose, mild protein elevation. Fungal/TB: lymphocytes, very low glucose, very high protein.

Bacterial meningitis would show PMN predominance (>80%), very low glucose (<40), and very high protein (>200). The lymphocytic predominance and glucose of 25 (borderline) are more consistent with viral meningitis.
TB meningitis presents with subacute course (weeks), very low glucose, very high protein (>200), and lymphocytic pleocytosis. This presentation is more acute and glucose is not low enough for TB.
Cryptococcal meningitis occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant). Opening pressure is often elevated. CSF shows low WBC, low glucose, and encapsulated yeasts on India ink.

rationale: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with low-normal glucose and elevated protein = viral/aseptic meningitis. Enterovirus is the most common cause.

question: A 65-year-old with diabetes presents with fever, urinary frequency, and suprapubic pain. Urine culture: ESBL-producing E. coli. What is the most appropriate antibiotic?

options.rationale: ESBL-producing organisms are resistant to all penicillins, cephalosporins, and often fluoroquinolones. Carbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem) are the drugs of choice. Clinical pearl: "ESBL treatment" — carbapenem is preferred for serious infections. Nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin can be used for uncomplicated cystitis from ESBL. Avoid ertapenem if the patient has received it recently (increased resistance risk).
ESBL-producing E. coli is resistant to ceftriaxone and ALL cephalosporins. Using ceftriaxone would be ineffective and potentially harmful (delaying effective therapy).
ESBL producers are often co-resistant to fluoroquinolones (up to 80% co-resistance). Sensitivity testing must guide therapy; empiric ciprofloxacin is not appropriate.

PT has variable activity against ESBL producers (inoculum effect — may appear sensitive in lab but fail in vivo). Meropenem is preferred for serious ESBL infections. PT is second-line for uncomplicated infections.

rationale: ESBL-producing organisms are resistant to all penicillins, cephalosporins, and often fluoroquinolones. Carbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem) are the drugs of choice.

question: A 45-year-old presents with fever, right flank pain, and dysuria. CT shows a 1.5 cm staghorn calculus in the renal pelvis. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV antibiotics + urgent decompression (percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteral stent)
options.rationale: Obstructive urolithiasis with infection (fever, flank pain) is a urologic emergency. Decompression is the priority along with IV antibiotics. Delayed decompression risks urosepsis and renal loss. Clinical pearl: "Obstructive pyelonephritis" — immediate drainage + IV antibiotics. Stones >2 cm or staghorn: PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy). Stones <2 cm: ESWL or ureteroscopy. Struvite stones from urease-producing organisms: complete removal essential.

options.text: IV antibiotics alone for 48h, then reassess
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone cannot clear infection with an obstructed urinary tract. The obstruction creates a closed space infection that requires drainage. The stone must be removed or bypassed.
Lithotripsy is elective treatment for non-infected renal stones. In the setting of acute infection, decompression is the priority, not stone fragmentation.
PCNL is the definitive stone treatment for staghorn calculi but is performed ELECTIVELY after infection is controlled, not during active pyelonephritis.

rationale: Obstructive urolithiasis with infection (fever, flank pain) is a urologic emergency. Decompression is the priority along with IV antibiotics.

question: A 50-year-old with classic hemophilia A (factor VIII <1%) presents with hemarthrosis of the right knee after minor trauma. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Recombinant factor VIII concentrate 40-50 U/kg IV
options.rationale: Hemophilia A with acute hemarthrosis requires factor VIII replacement to 40-80% of normal (moderate bleed). 1 U/kg raises FVIII by 2%. Target trough >50% for 48-72h. Clinical pearl: "Hemophilia management" — mild (FVIII >5%): DDAVP. Moderate/severe (FVIII <5%): factor concentrate. Inhibitors: bypassing agents (rFVIIa, FEIBA). Prophylaxis: regular factor infusions 3x/week starting at age 1-2 reduces joint bleeds and arthropathy.

DDAVP releases endogenous FVIII from endothelial stores but is only effective in MILD hemophilia A (FVIII >5%). In severe hemophilia (<1% FVIII), there is no FVIII to release. DDAVP is also ineffective in hemophilia B.
FFP contains all coagulation factors but in insufficient concentration to achieve therapeutic FVIII levels without volume overload. Cryoprecipitate or factor concentrate is preferred.
This patient has hemophilia A (FVIII deficiency). Factor IX treats hemophilia B (Christmas disease). Giving FIX to a hemophilia A patient provides no benefit.

rationale: Hemophilia A with acute hemarthrosis requires factor VIII replacement to 40-80% of normal (moderate bleed). 1 U/kg raises FVIII by 2%.

question: A 40-year-old presents with fever, headache, and myalgias for 3 days. He recently hiked in a forested area. He has a 3 cm erythematous rash with central clearing (erythema migrans). What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.rationale: Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) with erythema migrans is treated with doxycycline 100 mg BID or amoxicillin 500 mg TID for 14 days. Doxycycline is preferred as it also covers other tick-borne illnesses (anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis) that may co-infect. Clinical pearl: "Lyme disease stages" — early localized (EM rash): doxycycline. Early disseminated (multiple EM, carditis, facial palsy): doxycycline 14-28 days. Late (arthritis, neurologic): IV ceftriaxone 28 days.
IV ceftriaxone is reserved for late Lyme disease (Lyme arthritis, neuroborreliosis, AV block). Early localized disease is treated with oral antibiotics. IV therapy is unnecessarily aggressive for EM.
While amoxicillin is an alternative for Lyme disease, 10 days is insufficient. The recommended duration is 14 days. Doxycycline is preferred due to broader tick-borne coverage.
Untreated Lyme disease can progress to disseminated disease (arthritis, neurologic, cardiac complications). Antibiotic treatment prevents progression and reduces symptom duration.

rationale: Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) with erythema migrans is treated with doxycycline 100 mg BID or amoxicillin 500 mg TID for 14 days. Doxycycline is preferred as it also covers other tick-borne illnesses (anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis) that may co-infect.

question: A 55-year-old with cirrhosis develops fever and abdominal pain. Paracentesis: PMN 400 cells/mm³. Culture grows E. coli. What is the most appropriate management after antibiotics?

options.text: IV albumin 1.5g/kg at diagnosis + 1g/kg day 3 + secondary prophylaxis (norfloxacin/TMP-SMX)
options.rationale: SBP requires (1) IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone), (2) IV albumin to prevent HRS-AKI, (3) after resolution, daily norfloxacin or TMP-SMX for secondary prophylaxis. Clinical pearl: "SBP prophylaxis" — Primary prophylaxis: norfloxacin 400mg/day in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C, ascites protein <1.5g/dL, Cr >1.2, BUN >25, Na <130). Secondary prophylaxis: after first SBP episode, continue lifelong prophylaxis or until transplant.

options.text: IV albumin 25g + secondary prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin
options.rationale: The albumin dosing from the ANSWER trial is 1.5g/kg initially, then 1g/kg on day 3. A flat dose of 25g may be insufficient. Norfloxacin is preferred over ciprofloxacin for prophylaxis due to less resistance.
SBP recurrence rate without prophylaxis is 70% at 1 year. Secondary prophylaxis reduces recurrence to 20%. Lifelong prophylaxis is standard of care after a first SBP episode.
While SBP indicates advanced liver disease, transplant evaluation is arranged electively, not emergently. The immediate priority is treating the infection and initiating prophylaxis.

rationale: SBP requires (1) IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone), (2) IV albumin to prevent HRS-AKI, (3) after resolution, daily norfloxacin or TMP-SMX for secondary prophylaxis. Clinical pearl: "SBP prophylaxis" — Primary prophylaxis: norfloxacin 400mg/day in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C, ascites protein <1.5g/dL, Cr >1.2, BUN >25, Na <130).

question: A 60-year-old on methotrexate for RA presents with fever, cough, and progressive dyspnea. CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. He is on methotrexate 15 mg weekly. What is the first step?

options.text: Stop methotrexate + start empiric TMP-SMX for PJP coverage
options.rationale: Methotrexate-induced immunosuppression can predispose to opportunistic infections, including PJP. Methotrexate can also cause acute interstitial pneumonitis. Both require stopping methotrexate. Empiric PJP coverage with TMP-SMX is appropriate while diagnostic workup (BAL, PCR) is pending. Clinical pearl: "Methotrexate pneumonitis vs PJP" — both present with cough, fever, dyspnea, and interstitial infiltrates. If CD4 suspected low or steroid dose high, treat empirically for PJP while BAL results pending.

options.text: Increase methotrexate to 20 mg weekly and add steroids
options.rationale: Increasing immunosuppression in the setting of progressive pulmonary infiltrates would be harmful. The first step is to stop the suspected offending agent (methotrexate) and treat for possible infection.

options.text: CT chest with contrast and schedule bronchoscopy electively
options.rationale: This patient has progressive dyspnea and requires urgent evaluation and empiric therapy. Delaying treatment while scheduling elective procedures could lead to respiratory failure.

options.text: Start high-dose prednisone for suspected methotrexate pneumonitis
options.rationale: Without knowing whether this is pneumonitis (steroid-responsive) or PJP (steroids may worsen), empiric TMP-SMX should be started. If BAL is negative for PJP, steroids can be initiated for pneumonitis.

rationale: Methotrexate-induced immunosuppression can predispose to opportunistic infections, including PJP. Methotrexate can also cause acute interstitial pneumonitis.
